title: Veterinary Care Deserts What Is the Capacity and Where Is It
authors: Veterinary Care Deserts: What Is the Capacity and Where Is It?
journal: Journal of Shelter Medicine and Community Animal Health
citation: Veterinary Care Deserts: What Is the Capacity and Where Is It? Veterinary Care Deserts What Is the Capacity and Where Is It. 2022.
abstract: Introduction: Access to veterinary care is a complex issue that lies at the intersection of socioeconomics, culture, and space. Although there has been substantial research that has explored factors that impede access to care, the issue has not been well addressed from a geographic perspective. Access deserts is a familiar concept that has been applied to human health care, access to nutritious foods, etc. Thus, there is value in conceptualizing access to veterinary care through the same lens. This research aims to advance the effort of identifying veterinary care deserts by specifying normative values for two fundamental parameters: the ratio of care providers to measures of the population and the catchment of clinics. Methods: Total employees at veterinary clinics were aggregated at the county level and normalized by different measures of human and companion animal population. All clinic employees are included under the assumption that increased support staff increases the overall care capacity. Weighted means were generated and reported for each approach. The number of veterinary clinic employees needed in each county in order to reach the weighted mean for the overall country is also reported both at the county level and state level. Clinic catchment was measured by evaluating the mean distance traveled using data from a large number of clinics and clinic clients. The data were further analyzed using Rural Urban Commuting Areas (RUCA) classifications. Results: Veterinary employee shortages were observed ranging from 20,000 to 60,000 employees depending on how the data are viewed. Parameters for the weighted mean number of employees were reported in a detailed chart. Results of the distance analysis indicate that most people travel between 2 and 6 miles to reach clinics. Conclusion: This research indicates spatial disparities in the distribution of veterinary staff. The parameters of the ratio of employees to population measures and distance traveled can both be used in future research that aims to identify local and regional veterinary care deserts. This analysis could be further enhanced by the addition of factors such as socioeconomic data or social determinants of health to further define and identify care deserts. title: Veterinary Clinician's Opinions and Experiences with the Feline Ovarian Pedicle Tie
authors: Veterinary Clinician's Opinions and Experiences with the Feline Ovaria... https://jsmcah.org/index.php/jasv/article/view/51
journal: Journal of Shelter Medicine and Community Animal Health
citation: Veterinary Clinician's Opinions and Experiences with the Feline Ovaria... https://jsmcah.org/index.php/jasv/article/view/51 Veterinary Clinician's Opinions and Experiences with the Feline Ovarian Pedicle Tie. 2023. doi:10.56771/jsmcah.v2.51
abstract: Ligation of the feline ovarian pedicle is commonly performed by autoligation, also known as the pedicle tie. This technique is faster than double ligation with suture, has a very low risk of hemorrhage-related complications, and has been suggested as an acceptable standard in all practice settings. However, although it has been demonstrated to be appropriate for novice surgeons under supervision, fewer institutions teach autoligation than double ligation. This study aimed to determine the opinions and experiences of general practitioners regarding the feline ovarian pedicle tie. An anonymous 23-question online survey entitled “Veterinary Clinician's Opinions and Experiences with Surgical Spay/Neuter Techniques” was advertised to veterinarians performing feline ovariohysterectomies via social media posts that also encouraged sharing and cross-posting. The survey questions, most of which presented nonexclusive answer options resulting in percentages summing to greater than 100%, probed the opinions and experiences of veterinarians regarding the technique. There were 142 respondents, with 77 indicating the use of the pedicle tie and 65 indicating no use. Of those who used the pedicle tie, most reported learning from either a dedicated high-quality high volume (HQHV) educational setting (32%) or a colleague/ mentor (32%). Nearly half used it in all cases, although 20% did not use it for pregnant cats. They had used it for a median of 5 (IQ 3-8) years, and 99% were comfortable teaching the technique to others. Of those who did not use the pedicle tie, 60% reported that it meets the standard of care (SOC), 14% reported that it does not, and 26% that it sometimes meets SOC. Most veterinarians not performing the pedicle tie thought it was appropriate for unowned cats or cats in HQHV programs (77-82%), but only 55% thought it was appropriate for owned cats in general practice. The most common reasons given for not using the technique were that they had not learned it in vet school (51%), followed by the fact that they had not seen it used before (34%) and that while they had seen it done, they were nervous to try (28%). Seventy-four percent of those who did not use autoligation of the feline ovarian pedicle used autoligation of the testicular pedicle, either the pedicle tie (40%) or figure 8 (34%). Of those who believed that the pedicle tie does not meet SOC, 78% indicated it was because they had not seen it used, and 67% because it was not taught in vet school. However, 89% reported that an expensive commercially available device with similar positive attributes, specifically reduced procedure time, met SOC. Veterinarians using the pedicle tie graduated more recently (P = 0.040), with the median year of graduation in 2011 (IQR 2004-2016) as compared to 2007 (IQR 1998-2014). The greatest barrier to performing the technique or considering it SOC is a lack of familiarity with the method and the fact that it is not taught routinely in veterinary school. There is an encouraging trend, with more recent graduates being more likely to perform the technique; however, there remains an opportunity to increase use. The goal of this study was to evaluate the OC’s WCP, a cat management program, conducted in Florida from January 1, 2019, to December 1, 2023. Methods: Data from cats enrolled in the OC’s WCP were retrieved from electronic records and analyzed using descriptive statistics. Cat adopters were surveyed to assess satisfaction with their adoptions and to evaluate the broader outcomes of the program. Results: A total of 968 cats were enrolled in 5 years of the program. In total, 99% (n = 959) of the cats had a live release rate (959), where 90% (862) were ‘hired’ (adopted into non-traditional homes), 9.9% (95) were transferred to rescue groups (to be adopted into traditional homes), and 2 were returned to their original location (return to field). 85% of the adopters who responded to a post-adoption survey (329/387) were very or completely satisfied with their adopted cat’s performance, and only 10% (40/387) were not or were somewhat satisfied with their adopted cat’s performance. title: Who Cares Exploring the Demographics and Proportion of People Providing Care for Community Cats in Seven Study Communities in the United States
authors: Who Cares? Exploring the Demographics and Proportion
journal: Journal of Shelter Medicine and Community Animal Health
citation: Who Cares? Exploring the Demographics and Proportion Who Cares Exploring the Demographics and Proportion of People Providing Care for Community Cats in Seven Study Communities in the United States. 2024.
abstract: Introduction: While several studies have evaluated the demographics of pet ownership in the US, few studies have explored the demographics and proportion of the population that feed community cats. This research examines these questions in seven geographically diverse study communities. The concept of capacity for caring is advanced as a way to quantify a community’s ability and willingness to provide for community cats. Methods: A web-based panel survey was distributed and received 6,318 responses. The survey was administered in seven different study communities as part of a larger survey. Individuals were asked a series of demographic and socioeconomic questions as well as whether they fed community cats. Results: The profile of people feeding community cats is diverse with Black and Hispanic respondents emerging as more likely to feed cats than White respondents. Results indicate that an average of 30% of people feed community cats, and that most feed three or fewer cats. Significant variation in the proportion of people feeding cats is seen across the seven study communities, perhaps driven by the number of cats in the different communities. Confirming findings of previous studies, individuals who have pets of their own are also significantly more likely to feed community cats. Conclusion: The results indicate that communities have a relatively high capacity to care for community cats. This research also adds an equity perspective to programs aimed at removal of community cats from their spaces. Cat caregivers are diverse and generally reflect their respective communities. Policymakers should consider the impact to the cats and their caregivers before implementing programs that target removal of community cats from their outdoor homes. Keywords: community cats; feral cats; feeding cats; DEI I n the United States, stray cat intakes greatly exceed the number of owner surrendered intakes and contribute disproportionately to the number of the animals euthwho share their community.2 When considering programs such as returning socialized cats to the field, some groups may be concerned that there will not be anyone caring for the cats. One way to consider this is to explore a community’s Capacity for Caring, a measure of the potential proportion of the community that would provide for cats they do not own. title: Zoonotic and Non Zoonotic Intestinal Parasites in Shelter Dogs at Admission and Before Discharge

abstract: Introduction: The prevalence of intestinal parasites, notably zoonotic ascarids and hookworms, is higher in shelter dogs, compared to dogs in homes, making parasite control within shelter facilities a public health priority. Objective: The objective of the study reported here was to measure and compare the frequency of dogs infected with zoonotic or non-zoonotic intestinal parasites at admission and before discharge at a shelter facility. Methods: Ninety-two dogs were tested for diagnosis of intestinal parasites at admission and before discharge. Results: At admission, 50/92 (54%) dogs were diagnosed with intestinal parasites. Most dogs (43/50) were diagnosed with mono-infections with Ancylostoma spp., or co-infections with Ancylostoma spp. and Toxocara sp. or non-zoonotic parasites. Sixty-five dogs had a complete fecal study performed, which included an intake and exit sample analyzed for presence of parasite ova. Among the 65 study dogs, the frequency of dogs with intestinal parasites was lower before discharge (23 or 35%), compared to that at admission (33 or 50%) (P = 0.02). Fifty-one of 65 (78%) dogs were adopted, transferred to an outside rescue facility, or returned to their owners. Of these 51 dogs that left the shelter during the study period, 16/51 (31%) dogs were infected with intestinal parasites, and 8 of the 16 infected dogs were diagnosed with zoonotic parasites. Finally, among 37 dogs that tested negative and 28 that tested positive to zoonotic parasites at admission and re-tested later, four (11%) and six (21%) dogs, respectively, tested positive to zoonotic parasites when tested later. Conclusion: The frequency of shelter dogs infected with intestinal parasites at admission and before discharge was high (≥35%), and most infections were caused by Ancylostoma spp., an intestinal parasite in dogs that can be transmitted to humans, particularly children. We offer health policy options that shelter veterinarians/managers and local policymakers can consider for possible implementation and evaluation. title: decrease in proportion of sterilized dogs entering animal welfare organizations in the US post pandemic
authors: Samantha Hill, Lexis H. Ly 2, John Cornelison and Julie K. Levy
journal: Journal of Shelter Medicine and Community Animal Health
citation: Samantha Hill, Lexis H. Ly 2, John Cornelison and Julie K. Levy decrease in proportion of sterilized dogs entering animal welfare organizations in the US post pandemic. 2025.
abstract: Introduction: The SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) pandemic disrupted spay and neuter services for owned and unowned animals in the United States; however, the impact of this deficit on animal welfare organizations’ intake and capacity has not been reported. This study examined nationwide data for trends in sterilization status of dogs entering animal shelters and rescue organizations in 2019–2023. Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted using a national database for dogs admitted as owner surrenders or strays and outcomed to adoption in 2019–2023. Descriptive statistics were used for prealter status as a function of region, intake type, age, size, sex, and length of stay, and binary logistic regression to evaluate predictors of prealtered status. Results: A total of 1,136,021 dogs admitted to 256 U.S. shelters and rescues across 46 states and Washington D.C. met the study criteria. The proportion of dogs entering shelters prealtered declined from 33.2% in 2019 to 22.3% in 2023, with varied decreases across regions, intake types, and size groups. Prealtered dogs had shorter median length of stay to adoption compared to unaltered dogs. Multiple factors influenced the odds of a dog being prealtered. For example, there were higher odds of being prealtered among senior and male dogs, and lower odds among juveniles and stray dogs. Lower dog intake partially offset the total number of unaltered dogs admitted from 185,138 dogs in 2019 to 173,314 in 2023. Conclusion: The percentage of dogs prealtered at intake decreased year over year post-pandemic, which may impact time spent in care. Animal welfare organizations should consider assessing prealter status at intake to predict shelter capacity and identify trends in access to sterilization services. title: estimating the dog population, responsible pet ownership, and intestinal parasitism in dogs in quito, eccuador

abstract: Introduction: In 2011, authorities of Quito, the capital city of Ecuador, approved an ordinance to promote public health and animal welfare through responsible pet ownership promotion. The population of dogs was not known, and the relationships between dog abundance, socioeconomic factors, prevalence of zoonotic gastrointestinal parasites, and pet ownership responsibility had not been investigated. The objectives of this study were (1) to estimate the human:dog (HD) ratio, (2) to examine the relationship between household factors and responsible pet ownership, and (3) to estimate the prevalence of households with one or more dogs infected with intestinal parasites in Quito, Ecuador. Methods: Space-based random sampling procedures were used for estimation of HD ratios in free-roaming dogs and confined owned dogs. The relationship between household factors and a Responsible Pet Ownership Index was examined using logistic regression. Dog fecal samples were tested for intestinal parasites. Results: Among stray dogs, the observed HD ratio was 58:1. Among dogs kept indoors, the observed HD ratio was 3.5:1. A positive interaction effect between number of dogs in study households and household living conditions (a proxy for household wealth) on responsible pet ownership was observed, which we discuss in this report. Prevalence of households with dogs infected with intestinal parasites was 28% (95% confidence interval [CI] = 21–37). Ancylostoma spp. was the most frequent intestinal parasite in study dogs kept indoors. Conclusion: This study provides new information that can be used by policy makers to formulate, implement, and evaluate public policies and education programs aimed at enhancing animal welfare and health in Ecuador. title: “I‘m tired in my bones“_ Associations Between Adverse Childhood Experiences, Secondary Traumatic Stress, and Professional Quality of Life in Animal Shelter Workers
authors: Associations Between Adverse Childhood Experiences, Secondary Traumatic
journal: Journal of Shelter Medicine and Community Animal Health
citation: Associations Between Adverse Childhood Experiences, Secondary Traumatic “I‘m tired in my bones“_ Associations Between Adverse Childhood Experiences, Secondary Traumatic Stress, and Professional Quality of Life in Animal Shelter Workers. 2025. doi:10.56771/jsmcah.v4.137
abstract: Introduction Animal Shelter workers (ASW) provide direct care for animals that may be lost, homeless, neglected, or abused and may be at increased risk for occupational trauma.1 Animal shelter workers report higher anger, anxiety, depression and fatigue scores than the general population.2 Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) are traumatic or stressful events that occur during childhood, potentially impacting a person's health and well-being throughout their life. ACEs are quantified as a count of adverse events ranging from 0 to 10. A score of 4 or higher indicates a clinically significant increase in risk for mental health conditions, chronic physical diseases, substance abuse, and shortened lifespan, with the higher the score, the greater the risk.3 It is estimated that 5-10% of the general population has a score of at least 4. This study sought to determine whether there is an association between ACEs score, secondary traumatic stress, professional quality of life measures, and method of co-regulation. Methods University of Tennessee College of Veterinary Medicine (UTCVM) collaborated with veterinary social workers from the College of Social Work to provide an on-site “lunch and learn” aimed to provide strategies to improve the mental health and well-being of ASW. Animal shelters located throughout the Tennessee Valley and within a 65-mile radius of Knoxville, Tennessee, were eligible for inclusion, and all full or part-time ASWs were invited to participate, regardless of their position or length of employment. ASWs were invited to participate in a ten-minute survey that combined indicators of adverse childhood events, secondary traumatic stress, and professional quality of life as measured by the ACEs scale, Secondary Traumatic Stress Scale (STSS), and Professional Quality of Life (PQoL) tools, respectively. Correlations were measured using Spearman’s rho. Results Surveys were collected and analyzed from 134 ASWs from 15 animal shelters. Over 50% of the ASWs had an ACEs score of 4 or greater, with a mean of 4 (SD 2.7) and mode of 5 (n=24). ACEs were significantly correlated with STSS scores, both for the total (r = 0.4, P < 0.001) and on the subscales of intrusion (r = 0.3, P = 0.001), avoidance (r = 0.4, P < 0.001), and arousal (r = 0.4, P < 0.001). ACEs were also strongly correlated with PQoL) scores in burnout (r = 0.3, P < 0.001) and trauma (r = 0.4, P < 0.001), but not compassion (r=-0.1, p=0.433). As ACEs score increased, use of friends and family for emotional co-regulation decreased, both r = -0.2 and P = 0.006 and 0.023, respectively. Conclusion People who have more adverse childhood experiences may gravitate toward shelter work and rely more upon pets than family or friends for emotional co-regulation. ASW may benefit from mental health strategies that focus on self-compassion. title: Pets in Lower Socioeconomic Communities Have a Higher Exposure to Second-Hand Smoke

abstract: Animals living in the lowest socioeconomic Postal (ZIP) codes had a higher rate (26.7%) of positive urine cotinine compared to animals living in a higher income Postal (ZIP) code (4%). This study investigated whether animals in lower-income areas face greater secondhand smoke (SHS) exposure than pets in wealthier neighborhoods, examining urine samples from 168 animals across different socioeconomic ZIP codes and measuring cotinine levels as a smoke exposure indicator. The substantial difference suggests socioeconomic disparities in SHS exposure for companion animals. The authors conclude that given higher exposure rates in disadvantaged communities, efforts should focus on promoting smoking cessation and providing cessation resources.

title: Impact of Plasma Supplementation on Survival and Clinical Illness in Orphaned Neonatal Kittens in a Retrospective Shelter Cohort
authors: Chapman J, Piraino A, Min K, Diniz PPVP, Noble J, Hedge Z
journal: Journal of Shelter Medicine and Community Animal Health
citation: Chapman J, Piraino A, Min K, Diniz PPVP, Noble J, Hedge Z Impact of Plasma Supplementation on Survival and Clinical Illness in Orphaned Neonatal Kittens in a Retrospective Shelter Cohort. Journal of Shelter Medicine and Community Animal Health. 2026. doi:10.56771/jsmcah.v5.143
abstract: The San Diego Humane Society manages numerous orphaned kittens annually who face elevated illness and mortality risks. This retrospective cohort study examined whether subcutaneous plasma administration at intake affected outcomes in 544 orphaned kittens (193 receiving plasma, 351 controls) between February and August 2015. The investigation focused on two primary outcomes: mortality within 30 days and time until onset of clinical signs including diarrhea, upper respiratory infection, hypothermia, anorexia, weight loss, or neurological symptoms. Plasma supplementation was not statistically associated with decreased mortality risk at any time during the first 30 days despite early survival curve differences. However, plasma administration did delay onset of diarrhea and weight loss. The research identified intake weight and weight gain as the most important survival predictors, suggesting nutritional support's critical role in kitten outcomes within shelter settings.

mcqs.q: Should subcutaneous plasma supplementation be routinely recommended to improve survival in orphaned neonatal kittens in shelter settings?
o: Yes — plasma supplementation significantly reduces mortality within the first 30 days
Not definitively — plasma was not statistically associated with decreased mortality, though it did delay onset of diarrhea and weight loss
Yes — plasma supplementation improves both survival and speeds weight gain
No — plasma supplementation increased illness risk by introducing immunoglobulin overload
mcqs.e: In this retrospective cohort of 544 kittens, plasma supplementation was not statistically associated with decreased mortality at any time point in the first 30 days, despite early survival curve differences. However, plasma did delay the onset of diarrhea and weight loss. The strongest predictors of survival were intake weight and weight gain, highlighting the primacy of nutritional support over plasma supplementation in kitten care protocols.

mcqs.q: What are the most important predictors of survival in orphaned neonatal kittens cared for in a shelter setting?
o: Plasma supplementation at intake and absence of upper respiratory infection
Intake weight and subsequent weight gain — nutritional support is the critical determinant
Age at intake and body temperature on arrival
Whether kittens were littermates or singletons, as social support affects feeding behavior

Plasma supplementation did not reduce mortality, though it delayed some illness signs. This finding underscores that optimizing nutritional support — feeding protocols, frequency, formula type — should be the central focus of neonatal kitten care programs, rather than assuming plasma supplementation is a reliable life-saving intervention.

title: An Interview-Based Retrospective Study on Long-Term Outcomes of Shelter Cats with Feline Lower Urinary Tract Disease (FLUTD) and a History of Urethral Obstruction (UO)
authors: Mendoza K, Ferrell E, Rekers W
journal: Journal of Shelter Medicine and Community Animal Health
citation: Mendoza K, Ferrell E, Rekers W An Interview-Based Retrospective Study on Long-Term Outcomes of Shelter Cats with Feline Lower Urinary Tract Disease (FLUTD) and a History of Urethral Obstruction (UO). Journal of Shelter Medicine and Community Animal Health. 2026. doi:10.56771/jsmcah.v5.169
abstract: Historical shelter practices have sometimes involved euthanasia for cats with FLUTD and urethral obstruction due to concerns about adoptability and prognosis. While recurrent urinary issues occur in up to 51% of affected cats and obstruction recurs in 15-47%, this retrospective study examined actual adoption outcomes. Researchers surveyed adopters of 78 shelter cats with prior obstruction, achieving a 39.7% response rate. Inclusion required at least one documented obstruction event requiring 24+ hours of catheterization, absence of other conditions, successful adoption, and minimum three-month residence post-event. All cats were alive and remained in their adopted homes with only 32.3% showing recurrent symptoms and 6.5% experiencing re-obstruction. Housing environment, household composition, and diet showed no statistical association with recurrence. All respondents expressed willingness to adopt similar cats again, indicating positive experiences and favorable long-term outcomes despite study limitations.

mcqs.q: Should shelter cats with a history of urethral obstruction be considered poor adoption candidates with a high likelihood of recurrence requiring euthanasia?
o: Yes — recurrent obstruction affects the majority of cats and most adopters report dissatisfaction with the experience
No — long-term outcomes are favorable: all cats remained alive and in their adopted homes, with only a minority showing recurrent symptoms
Only cats with a single obstruction event have good long-term outcomes; multiple obstruction events predict poor prognosis
Outcomes depend entirely on diet — cats fed wet food exclusively show no recurrence
mcqs.e: Despite documented recurrence rates of urinary issues in up to 51% and re-obstruction in 15–47% of affected cats in the literature, this study of 78 adopted shelter cats with prior obstruction found that all cats were alive and remained in their adopted homes. Only 32.3% showed recurrent urinary symptoms and only 6.5% experienced re-obstruction. All adopters expressed willingness to adopt similar cats again. Historical euthanasia for this condition appears unjustified based on actual long-term outcomes.

mcqs.q: An adopter is told a cat has previously been obstructed and asks about the likelihood of serious recurrence. What is the evidence-based answer?
o: Re-obstruction is nearly universal — most cats obstructs again within 6 months and require ongoing intensive management

mcqs.e: In this study, only 6.5% of adopted cats with prior obstruction experienced re-obstruction, and 32.3% had any recurrent urinary symptoms. Household environment, composition, and diet showed no statistical association with recurrence. All adopters would adopt a similar cat again. Clients should be counseled that re-obstruction is uncommon and that quality of life for these cats is generally excellent after adoption.

title: Who Let the Dogs Out? A Cross-Sectional Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices Survey Reveals Caregiver Behavior and a Value-Action Gap in Ownership Practices as Potential Contributors to Free-Roaming Dog Populations in Fiji
authors: Quimby C, Dhillon J, Tunabuna TN, Hoopes JH
journal: Journal of Shelter Medicine and Community Animal Health
citation: Quimby C, Dhillon J, Tunabuna TN, Hoopes JH Who Let the Dogs Out? A Cross-Sectional Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices Survey Reveals Caregiver Behavior and a Value-Action Gap in Ownership Practices as Potential Contributors to Free-Roaming Dog Populations in Fiji. Journal of Shelter Medicine and Community Animal Health. 2026. doi:10.56771/jsmcah.v5.166
abstract: This research examined dog population dynamics in Fiji through household surveys. The investigators found that 37% of households owned dogs for protection or companionship, while 54% fed stray animals. Despite favorable attitudes toward sterilization and licensing, uptake remained minimal due to awareness gaps. High levels of caregiver behavior and community dog feeding, compounded by low desexing rates contributed to the free-roaming dog problem. The study identified a significant disconnect between what residents valued and their actual practices—people expressed support for preventive care but failed to implement these measures consistently. The researchers concluded that traditional control methods like culling misaligned with community preferences, and recommended community-driven, evidence-based approaches to responsible ownership as essential for effective dog population management programs.

mcqs.q: A KAP survey in Fiji found that most residents expressed positive attitudes toward dog sterilization and licensing, yet uptake of both practices remained very low. What concept does this exemplify, and what does it suggest about intervention strategy?
o: This illustrates a knowledge deficit—residents lack information about sterilization, so mass awareness campaigns are the primary intervention needed
This illustrates a value-action gap—positive attitudes do not translate to behavior—indicating that awareness alone is insufficient and community-driven, barrier-reducing approaches are needed
This reflects community opposition to sterilization that is masked by socially desirable survey responses
The gap between attitudes and practices is typical and resolves over time without targeted intervention
mcqs.e: The study explicitly identified a 'value-action gap': residents supported preventive care in principle but failed to implement it. The authors concluded that awareness gaps (not just knowledge deficits) and practical barriers underlie this gap, and recommended community-driven, evidence-based approaches rather than traditional punitive measures like culling.

mcqs.q: The Fiji survey found that 54% of households fed stray animals and that traditional control measures like culling were misaligned with community preferences. What is the most evidence-supported recommendation from this study for managing free-roaming dog populations?
o: Implement stricter culling enforcement, since community preference data are not a reliable guide to policy

Adopt community-driven, humane approaches to responsible ownership that align with residents' stated values and address practical barriers to sterilization and containment

mcqs.e: The study found that community feeding of strays, low desexing rates, and a value-action gap all contributed to free-roaming dog populations. The authors recommended community-driven, evidence-based approaches to responsible ownership that align with community values—since culling was misaligned with preferences and therefore likely to face poor compliance.

title: A Descriptive Survey of Visitor Experience and Adoption Interest Among Patrons of a Rabbit Café

abstract: The researchers investigated visitor motivations and experiences at a rabbit café in Vancouver, British Columbia, collecting 205 visitor survey responses and 23 staff evaluations of rabbit sociability. Their findings revealed that most visitors did not intend to adopt rabbits, but mainly visited the café to spend time with animals, valuing hands-on interaction as meaningful. The study noted that rabbits rated as highly social by staff were generally preferred over shy individuals. While the café provided an enjoyable venue for human-animal contact, it did not result in adoptions during the study period. The authors suggest future research should examine strategies to enhance adoption outcomes and visitor duration at similar facilities.

No adoptions occurred during the study period. This suggests cafés provide human-animal contact benefits but are not reliable adoption pipelines without additional targeted strategies.

title: Comparison of the Number of Dog Adoptions in a Pilot Program That Restored Limited Visitor Access to Kennels: A Community Case Report

abstract: During 2020-2022, Orange County's animal shelter operated an appointment-only adoption system without kennel access. A 2023 pilot initiative allowed visitors to observe certain large dogs in their kennels during limited hours. The study found substantially higher adoptions during viewing periods compared to other times. Specifically, kennel viewing periods showed an 82% increase in adoptions while appointment-only periods showed only a 4% increase relative to the prior year's same calendar period. Additionally, viewable kennels produced a disproportionately high adoption rate for large dogs. The authors acknowledge important limitations: this was not randomized research, relied on retrospective data comparison, and results may not generalize to expanded access scenarios or longer operating hours.

title: Financial Hardship Assistance and Its Impact on Veterinary Care for Sick or Urgent Companion Animal Cases
authors: Harmon L, Kreisler R

abstract: The study examined veterinary hardship fund applications at Midwestern University's Companion Animal Clinic. Among 45 cases, 28 involved sick or urgent conditions. Treatment modifications due to finances occurred in 25% of cases despite hardship fund support. The hardship fund provided a median of $499 while clients contributed $0 (median). Importantly, no animals were euthanized for economic reasons. The findings demonstrate that financial hardship assistance can play a critical role in facilitating access to veterinary care, highlighting the importance of such programs for enabling treatment in urgent companion animal situations.

Economic euthanasia rates were not measured in this study

title: Principles of Veterinary Community Engagement: First Edition 2024
authors: Watson B, Berliner E, DeTar L, McCobb E, Frahm-Gilles W, Henry E, King E, Powell L, Reinhard C, Stavisky J

The guidelines aim to improve understanding of program design, implementation, and sustainability challenges while safeguarding animal dignity and welfare. title: Behavioral rehabilitation of extremely fearful dogs: Report on the efficacy of a treatment protocol
authors: Collins K, Miller K, Zverina L, Patterson-Kane E, Cussen V, Reid P
journal: Applied Animal Behaviour Science
citation: Collins K, Miller K, Zverina L, Patterson-Kane E, Cussen V, Reid P Behavioral rehabilitation of extremely fearful dogs: Report on the efficacy of a treatment protocol. Applied Animal Behaviour Science. 2022. doi:10.1016/j.applanim.2022.105689
abstract: Some dogs entering shelters exhibit extreme fearfulness, often after experiencing cruelty or neglect. Dogs displaying extreme fearfulness are difficult to assess and treat using the tools and protocols available in most shelters. Without effective treatment, these dogs have an unacceptably poor quality of life and are unlikely to be successfully adopted. Treatment protocols using behavior modification techniques such as desensitization, counterconditioning and operant conditioning were developed to reduce fear of stimuli that pet dogs typically experience in adoptive homes. From 2013–2020, outcomes were recorded for dogs that went through this behavioral rehabilitation program. The graduation rate from the program was 86 % (380/441). Graduated dogs spent an average of 96 (SD=55) days in the program, experiencing an average of 78 specific treatment sessions. They showed a significant improvement in behavior in a standardized behavior assessment (df=440, t = 28.3836, p = 0.001) before meeting criteria for placement. Once offered for adoption, they had a 99 % adoption rate and a 96 % adopter satisfaction rate. These results indicate that an appropriately designed behavioral rehabilitation program for dogs displaying extreme fear in a shelter setting can prove highly successful, resulting in improved quality of life and reduced need for behavioral euthanasia.

mcqs.q: Can extremely fearful dogs in shelter settings achieve successful adoption outcomes through structured behavioral rehabilitation programs?
o: Rarely — fear-based behavioral problems in shelter dogs are largely refractory to treatment and most dogs require euthanasia
Yes — a structured rehabilitation program using desensitization, counterconditioning, and operant conditioning achieved an 86% graduation rate, 99% adoption rate, and 96% adopter satisfaction
Outcomes are unpredictable and depend primarily on the dog's age and original trauma history
Rehabilitation is only effective for dogs with fear limited to specific stimuli, not generalized fearfulness
mcqs.e: From 2013–2020, 380 of 441 extremely fearful dogs graduated (86% graduation rate) from a structured behavioral rehabilitation program using behavior modification techniques. Graduated dogs spent an average of 96 days with ~78 treatment sessions. Of dogs offered for adoption, 99% were adopted and adopter satisfaction was 96%. These results demonstrate that with appropriate investment, behavioral euthanasia can be substantially reduced even for dogs with extreme fearfulness.

mcqs.q: What does the evidence suggest about behavioral euthanasia for extremely fearful dogs entering shelters?
o: Behavioral euthanasia remains the most humane option for dogs with extreme fearfulness, as quality of life cannot be meaningfully improved
Structured behavioral rehabilitation can significantly reduce the need for behavioral euthanasia, with the majority of extremely fearful dogs graduating and achieving successful adoption
Behavioral euthanasia should be reserved only for dogs that fail pharmacological treatment, not behavior modification
Fearful dogs improve spontaneously over time in shelter settings without structured intervention
mcqs.e: The 86% graduation rate, 99% adoption rate, and 96% adopter satisfaction from this long-term outcomes study demonstrate that behavioral euthanasia is not inevitable for extremely fearful dogs. However, the program required significant resources: an average of 96 days and 78 treatment sessions per dog. The study highlights that the primary barrier is resource allocation, not the futility of treatment — challenging the assumption that euthanasia is the most compassionate default.

title: Too much too soon? Risk factors for fear behaviour in foster kittens prior to adoption
authors: Graham C, Pearl DL, Niel L
journal: Applied Animal Behaviour Science
citation: Graham C, Pearl DL, Niel L Too much too soon? Risk factors for fear behaviour in foster kittens prior to adoption. Applied Animal Behaviour Science. 2024. doi:10.1016/j.applanim.2023.106141
abstract: Many companion kittens spend their sensitive period for socialization (~2–9 weeks of age) in foster care, and the quality of these early life experiences can impact behavioural development. This study aimed to improve early kitten care by using an online survey to investigate risk factors for fear behaviour in foster kittens prior to adoption (7–9 weeks of age) based on early management practices, foster parent personality traits, and evaluations of kitten behaviour. The main behavioural outcomes of this study were whether kittens showed caregiver-reported fear behaviour during interactions with unfamiliar people and unfamiliar objects just prior to adoption. Fear behaviour included displays of avoidance, freezing, crouching, ears back, piloerection, and aggression. We analyzed the impacts of kitten (n=235) and foster parent (n=72) characteristics, exposure to social stimuli (i.e., general handling, mimicking handling during a vet visit, exposure to people), and exposure to non-social stimuli (e.g., interactive toys, scratching material, different surfaces, etc.) provided. Using mixed logistic regression models, with foster parent as a random intercept to account for clustering at the foster home level, we found that kittens who were reported fearful at intake into foster care had significantly greater odds of displaying fear behaviours towards unfamiliar people and unfamiliar objects than kittens who were not reported fearful at intake. Additionally, kittens who received exposure to cognitive enrichment-based non-social stimuli had greater odds of displaying fear towards people compared to kittens who did not receive cognitive exposure. Kittens whose foster parent had a high score for emotional stability had greater odds of displaying fear towards people compared to those who had a low score for emotional stability. Further, kittens who received high exposure to social stimuli had reduced odds of displaying fear towards people than kittens who received low social exposure, as predicted. Some of these findings challenge recommendations for high amounts of exposure to social and non-social stimuli during early socialization. High social exposure was ineffective at reducing fear levels towards unfamiliar objects, and high cognitive enrichment-based non-social exposure appears to have exceeded kitten limits for optimal behavioural development. While appropriate socialization is beneficial for development, the current study highlights the need for further research to understand the impact of different socialization practices on kitten behavioural development, and the importance of accurately identifying when kittens are fearful and adapting socialization practices appropriately.

mcqs.q: In foster kittens, which single factor was most strongly associated with displaying fear behaviour toward unfamiliar people near the time of adoption?
o: Having a high-scoring emotional stability foster parent
Being housed with other kittens rather than as a singleton
Being reported as fearful at the time of intake into foster care
Receiving high levels of cognitive enrichment with non-social stimuli
mcqs.e: Kittens who were reported fearful at intake into foster care had significantly greater odds of displaying fear behaviour toward both unfamiliar people and unfamiliar objects at adoption age — the strongest predictor found in the study.

mcqs.q: This study found that kittens who received more social stimuli exposure (handling, interactions with people) during fostering had reduced odds of fear toward people. What is the practical take-home for foster kitten programmes?
o: Foster kittens should be kept in quiet, low-stimulation environments to avoid overwhelming them
Maximising early social exposure to people during fostering reduces fear behaviour prior to adoption
Social exposure should be delayed until kittens are older than 9 weeks to be effective
Foster parent personality is a stronger determinant of kitten socialisation than handling practices
mcqs.e: High social stimuli exposure — general handling, people interactions, mimicking vet handling — was associated with reduced odds of fear toward people. This supports active socialisation protocols during the sensitive period (2–9 weeks) in foster homes.

title: Behavior and adoptability of hoarded cats admitted to an animal shelter
authors: Jacobson LS, Ellis JJ, Janke KJ, Giacinti JA, Robertson JV
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
citation: Jacobson LS, Ellis JJ, Janke KJ, Giacinti JA, Robertson JV Behavior and adoptability of hoarded cats admitted to an animal shelter. Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery. 2022. doi:10.1177/1098612X221102122
abstract: The study examined behavioral characteristics and adoption success for previously hoarded cats. Researchers analyzed shelter records and post-adoption surveys from 195 hoarded cats (≥6 months old at intake), of which 174 were adopted. Key findings included: 52% scored as 'friendly' at intake; socialization scores showed 87% were 'supersocial' or 'social' after shelter habituation, declining to 47% immediately post-adoption, then recovering to 84% more than a week after adoption. Most cats scoring 'tense' at intake showed improved socialization later. Out-of-box elimination was uncommon (only 1 of 88 cats exhibited it in both settings). Adopters expressed positive feelings for 42 of 43 cats surveyed. Return rates did not differ significantly between hoarded (10%) and non-hoarded (7.1%) cats, nor did behavioral return reasons. The authors conclude that hoarded cats demonstrated high adoptability and adoption satisfaction, suggesting behavior-based decisions should be deferred to allow habituation time.

mcqs.q: Hoarded cats often appear tense or asocial in the shelter. What happened to their socialization scores over time, and what does this imply for adoption screening?
o: Socialization scores declined progressively, supporting early behavior-based screening to exclude fearful cats
Socialization scores were stable throughout, so shelter behavior reliably reflects adoptive home behavior
Scores recovered to near-shelter levels (84% social/supersocial) more than a week post-adoption, suggesting behavior-based exclusions should be deferred
Scores were high immediately post-adoption and declined over time, indicating a honeymoon effect
mcqs.e: Socialization dropped from 87% in-shelter to 47% immediately post-adoption (transition stress), then recovered to 84% after one week. The authors conclude that behavior-based decisions should be deferred to allow habituation — in-shelter scores do not predict long-term adoptive home behavior.

mcqs.q: How did return rates and reasons compare between hoarded and non-hoarded cats in this shelter study?
o: Hoarded cats had significantly higher return rates due to elimination problems
Hoarded cats had significantly higher behavioral return rates, justifying stricter adoption screening
Return rates and behavioral return reasons did not differ significantly between hoarded and non-hoarded cats
Non-hoarded cats had higher return rates due to medical issues that emerged post-adoption
mcqs.e: Return rates were 10% for hoarded vs. 7.1% for non-hoarded cats — not a statistically significant difference — and behavioral return reasons were also similar. This supports treating hoarded cats as adoptable rather than a high-risk population requiring special exclusion criteria.

mcqs.q: Out-of-box elimination is a common adoption concern for cats. What did this study find about elimination behavior in hoarded cats post-adoption?
o: Out-of-box elimination was common, occurring in the majority of adopted hoarded cats
Out-of-box elimination was uncommon, observed in only 1 of 88 cats in both shelter and home settings
Out-of-box elimination occurred in 30% of hoarded cats but resolved within 2 weeks of adoption
Hoarded cats had significantly higher elimination problems than non-hoarded cats
mcqs.e: Only 1 of 88 cats exhibited out-of-box elimination in both settings. This finding directly counters the concern that hoarding-background cats are prone to elimination problems, supporting their candidacy for adoption without elimination-specific screening.

title: Outbreak management of multidrug-resistant Bordetella bronchiseptica in 16 shelter-housed cats
authors: Rodriguez L, Berliner EA
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
citation: Rodriguez L, Berliner EA Outbreak management of multidrug-resistant Bordetella bronchiseptica in 16 shelter-housed cats. Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery. 2023. doi:10.1177/1098612X231153051
abstract: This case series examines an outbreak of multidrug-resistant Bordetella bronchiseptica affecting 16 shelter cats with respiratory illness. Four cats presented with acute breathing difficulty, each with prior upper respiratory disease history. Early diagnostic testing and culture and sensitivity allowed for targeted antimicrobial therapy and environmental interventions. Twelve additional presumptive cases were identified using exposure and clinical criteria. The comprehensive response included diagnostic protocols, risk evaluation, vaccination, isolation measures, heightened monitoring, and biosecurity review. The outbreak resolved within 26 days. The study notes this represents the first documented management of an MDR Bordetella bronchiseptica outbreak in shelter cats. The authors emphasize that early use of necropsy, PCR testing, and bacterial culture enabled rapid deployment of effective second-line antibiotics, and stress the importance of outbreak expertise and antimicrobial stewardship in resource-limited shelter settings.

mcqs.q: When managing a multidrug-resistant Bordetella bronchiseptica outbreak in shelter cats, what early intervention was most critical for effective treatment?
o: Initiating empirical first-line antibiotics (doxycycline or azithromycin) immediately without waiting for culture results
Early culture and sensitivity testing to guide targeted second-line antibiotic selection
Mass vaccination of all shelter cats with intranasal Bordetella vaccine at outbreak recognition
Immediate euthanasia of all confirmed MDR-positive cats to prevent further spread
mcqs.e: In an MDR Bordetella outbreak, standard first-line antibiotics will fail by definition. Early necropsy, PCR, and bacterial culture with sensitivity testing enabled rapid deployment of effective second-line antibiotics — the key step that resolved the outbreak in 26 days. This case underscores antimicrobial stewardship and early diagnostics in shelter respiratory outbreaks.

mcqs.q: The first documented MDR Bordetella bronchiseptica outbreak in shelter cats resolved within 26 days. What is the single most important management principle it illustrates?
o: Shelter respiratory outbreaks are best managed by depopulation rather than treatment
Routine empirical antibiotic prophylaxis prevents MDR Bordetella outbreaks in shelter populations
Early diagnostic investment (culture and sensitivity) and antimicrobial stewardship are essential, even in resource-limited shelters
MDR respiratory pathogens are too difficult to manage in shelters; transfer to foster is always preferred
mcqs.e: The authors explicitly stress antimicrobial stewardship and early diagnostic use as essential, even in resource-limited shelter settings. The successful 26-day resolution without euthanizing affected cats demonstrates that MDR respiratory outbreaks are manageable when diagnosed and treated appropriately from the outset.

title: Diagnostic testing for feline panleukopenia in a shelter setting: a prospective, observational study
authors: Jacobson LS, Janke KJ, Giacinti J, Weese JS
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
citation: Jacobson LS, Janke KJ, Giacinti J, Weese JS Diagnostic testing for feline panleukopenia in a shelter setting: a prospective, observational study. Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery. 2021. doi:10.1177/1098612X211005301
abstract: This shelter-based investigation evaluated diagnostic approaches for feline panleukopenia virus (FPV) infection. Researchers compared point-of-care SNAP testing with quantitative real-time PCR, assessed alternative sample types (vomit, swabs), and clarified interpretation of weak-positive results. Among 145 cats, 17 had confirmed FPV infection and 62 tested negative. Fecal SNAP sensitivity reached 55%, while vomit PCR achieved 100% (n=17; 95% CI 16-100). Overall specificity remained high across all methods (96-100%). The analysis revealed that positive SNAP results, including weak positives, correlated with higher viral copy numbers than false-negative results. The authors conclude that SNAP testing functions as an initial screening tool. Positive fecal results—including weak positives—are reliable indicators in symptomatic animals, but negative results require PCR confirmation before ruling out FPV infection.

mcqs.q: For diagnosing feline panleukopenia in a shelter, what is the correct interpretation of a negative fecal SNAP test result in a symptomatic cat?
o: A negative fecal SNAP reliably rules out FPV infection and the cat can return to the general population
A negative fecal SNAP does not rule out FPV infection and PCR confirmation is needed before excluding the diagnosis
A negative SNAP test should prompt immediate retesting with a different antigen platform
A negative SNAP test is more reliable than PCR for ruling out FPV in symptomatic shelter cats
mcqs.e: Fecal SNAP sensitivity for FPV was only 55% — meaning nearly half of infected cats would be missed by SNAP alone. Negative SNAP results in symptomatic animals require PCR confirmation. Vomit PCR achieved 100% sensitivity, though it is less routinely used.

mcqs.q: A shelter cat tests weakly positive on fecal SNAP for panleukopenia. How should this result be interpreted?
o: Weak positives are likely due to post-vaccination shedding and should not trigger isolation
Weak positives are unreliable and should be repeated three times before acting on the result
In symptomatic cats, a weak positive is a reliable indicator of infection and should be treated accordingly
Weak positives indicate early infection before antibody titers rise, not active viral disease
mcqs.e: Weak-positive SNAP results correlated with higher viral copy numbers than false-negative results. In symptomatic animals, positive SNAP results — including weak positives — are reliable indicators of FPV infection. This is distinct from post-vaccination PCR shedding, where the point-of-care antigen test typically remains negative.

title: Fecal viral DNA shedding following clinical panleukopenia virus infection in shelter kittens: a prospective, observational study
authors: Janke KJ, Jacobson LS, Giacinti JA, Weese JS
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
citation: Janke KJ, Jacobson LS, Giacinti JA, Weese JS Fecal viral DNA shedding following clinical panleukopenia virus infection in shelter kittens: a prospective, observational study. Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery. 2022. doi:10.1177/1098612X211023056
abstract: The research investigated the extent and timeline of fecal viral DNA shedding in shelter cats diagnosed with feline panleukopenia using quantitative real-time PCR. Researchers followed 40 cats and kittens over a 21-day period, testing fecal samples on days 0, 3, 7, 14, and 21. Key findings indicated that median DNA viral copy numbers fell below the diagnostic cut-off by day 7 with decreasing PCR positivity rates across the observation period. The study found that SNAP test results, diarrhea and systemic signs were inconsistent in relation to qPCR positivity. The authors recommended that infected cats should remain isolated for at least 14 days following diagnosis, after which release could be considered as part of a comprehensive infection control approach.

mcqs.q: For how long should shelter cats recovering from clinical panleukopenia remain isolated, based on fecal shedding data?
o: At least 48 hours after clinical signs resolve
At least 7 days after diagnosis, when SNAP tests become negative
At least 14 days after diagnosis, after which release can be considered as part of a comprehensive infection control approach
At least 21 days after diagnosis, until PCR is confirmed negative on two consecutive tests
mcqs.e: Median fecal viral DNA copy numbers fell below the diagnostic cut-off by day 7, but PCR positivity rates continued to decrease through day 14. The authors recommend at least 14 days of isolation following diagnosis before considering release, with qPCR results and clinical signs considered together in the decision.

mcqs.q: When using qPCR to guide release decisions for panleukopenia-recovering shelter cats, what important caveat applies?
o: qPCR is too insensitive for routine shelter use and should be replaced by SNAP testing for release decisions
qPCR positivity, diarrhea, and systemic signs do not consistently correlate, so clinical signs alone cannot reliably determine when PCR-based release criteria are met
qPCR results must always be paired with serology to accurately determine the end of the infectious period
qPCR automatically differentiates vaccine virus shedding from natural FPV infection in clinically affected cats
mcqs.e: SNAP test results, diarrhea, and systemic signs were inconsistent in relation to qPCR positivity across the study period. This means clinical resolution alone cannot substitute for time-based isolation protocols; the 14-day post-diagnosis minimum accounts for this inconsistency in shed-versus-signs correlation.

title: Effect of a provincial feline onychectomy ban on cat intake and euthanasia in a British Columbia animal shelter system
authors: Ellis A, van Haaften K, Protopopova A, Gordon E
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
citation: Ellis A, van Haaften K, Protopopova A, Gordon E Effect of a provincial feline onychectomy ban on cat intake and euthanasia in a British Columbia animal shelter system. Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery. 2022. doi:10.1177/1098612X211043820
abstract: This research examined whether a provincial ban on elective cat declawing affected shelter intake and euthanasia outcomes. The study analyzed British Columbia SPCA records from 36 months before (May 2015–April 2018; n=41,157) and after (May 2018–April 2021; n=33,430) the provincial ban on onychectomy. Destructive behavior was found to be an uncommon reason for surrender (0.18% of surrendered cats) during the study period. There was no statistically significant difference in the number of cats surrendered for destructive scratching behavior after the provincial ban on elective onychectomy. The proportion of owner-requested euthanasias decreased after the ban. The total number of cats surrendered, the shelter live release rate and average length of stay all remained stable or improved following the ban, though causation could not be determined.

mcqs.q: After a provincial ban on elective cat onychectomy (declawing), what happened to shelter cat intake and outcomes in British Columbia SPCA shelters?
o: Cat intake increased significantly as owners surrendered cats they could no longer declaw
No significant increase in surrenders for destructive scratching was detected, and live release rate and length of stay remained stable or improved
Intake for destructive behavior increased substantially, but was offset by a rise in adoptions
The ban led to a significant increase in owner-requested euthanasia for scratching behavior
mcqs.e: Analysis of BC SPCA records from 36 months before and after the ban found no statistically significant increase in cats surrendered for destructive scratching (which was already rare at 0.18% of surrendered cats). Owner-requested euthanasias actually decreased after the ban. Total intake, live release rate, and length of stay remained stable or improved. The ban did not negatively impact shelter outcomes.

mcqs.q: What proportion of cats surrendered to BC SPCA shelters cited destructive scratching behavior as the reason, both before and after the onychectomy ban?
o: Approximately 15–20% — scratching is a leading reason for cat surrender
Approximately 0.18% — destructive behavior was a rare reason for surrender throughout the study period
This increased from about 1% to 5% after the ban was implemented
Approximately 5%, stable before and after the ban
mcqs.e: Destructive scratching was cited as the reason for surrender in only 0.18% of cats during the study period, and there was no statistically significant difference after the ban. This is a critical finding for policy discussions: the assumption that banning declawing will flood shelters with cats surrendered for scratching is not supported by evidence from a large, real-world dataset.

title: Guidance for management of free-roaming community cats: a bioeconomic analysis
authors: Benka VA, Boone JD, Miller PS, Briggs JR, Anderson AM, Slootmaker C, Slater M, Levy JK, Nutter FB, Zawistowski S
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
citation: Benka VA, Boone JD, Miller PS, Briggs JR, Anderson AM, Slootmaker C, Slater M, Levy JK, Nutter FB, Zawistowski S Guidance for management of free-roaming community cats: a bioeconomic analysis. Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery. 2022. doi:10.1177/1098612X211055685
abstract: This study employed computer modeling to evaluate various free-roaming cat management approaches and their expense-effectiveness. The research examined lethal removal, non-lethal removal, trap-neuter-return, combination strategies, and no intervention using stochastic simulation. Results indicated that cost-effective reduction of free-roaming cat numbers required sufficient management intensity, regardless of management approach. The findings showed removal produced faster initial population declines, though sterilization-based methods proved potentially more economical at higher intensities. Among five scenarios achieving comparable 45% population reductions, strategies emphasizing sterilization cost substantially less than removal-only approaches, offering communities evidence-based frameworks for developing informed management policies.

mcqs.q: A bioeconomic model compared lethal removal, TNR, combination strategies, and no intervention for free-roaming cat management. What was the key finding about the relationship between program intensity and effectiveness?
o: Low-intensity programs of any type are sufficient for cost-effective population reduction if sustained over many years
Cost-effective population reduction requires sufficient management intensity regardless of the approach used; underpowered programs of any type are inefficient
Lethal removal is always the most cost-effective strategy at all intensity levels
TNR is only cost-effective in small, closed populations and should not be used in open urban cat colonies
mcqs.e: The model showed that intensity—not just approach—was the critical variable. Insufficient intensity made all strategies cost-ineffective. This is a key planning principle: committing to a program at scale is more important than choosing between removal and TNR at low coverage.

mcqs.q: The bioeconomic model found that among five strategies achieving a comparable 45% population reduction, sterilization-based approaches cost substantially less than removal-only. How should this inform community decision-making about free-roaming cat management?
o: Removal should be chosen when fast initial population decline is needed, even if long-term costs are higher; TNR should only be considered when cost is the overriding priority

When comparable population outcomes can be achieved, sterilization-based programs offer a cost advantage over removal-only approaches, making them the more economical choice at equivalent effectiveness
The cost advantage of sterilization is only realized when combined with lethal removal in a hybrid program
Because modeling assumptions may not reflect field conditions, cost comparisons between removal and TNR should be disregarded by communities
mcqs.e: Among strategies producing equivalent outcomes, sterilization-based approaches cost substantially less than removal-only. Communities facing resource constraints and seeking sustained population reduction have an evidence-based economic argument for sterilization-centered programs.

mcqs.q: The bioeconomic model found that removal produces faster initial population declines than sterilization-based approaches, yet sterilization proved more economical at higher program intensities. What is the most important practical implication of this trade-off for communities planning free-roaming cat management?
o: Communities should always choose removal because speed of population decline outweighs cost considerations

Communities that prioritise long-term cost-effectiveness and can sustain high program intensity have an economic argument for sterilization-based approaches, even though removal achieves faster initial results
Removal and sterilization are equivalent on both speed and cost at all intensity levels, so the choice is arbitrary
Sterilization-based methods are only economical when combined with lethal removal in a hybrid program
mcqs.e: The model showed removal achieves faster initial population declines, but sterilization-based strategies proved potentially more economical at higher program intensities. Among five scenarios achieving comparable 45% reductions, sterilization cost substantially less than removal-only. Communities can use this evidence to weigh speed of decline against long-term cost when choosing management approaches.

title: Ear-tipping practices for identification of cats sterilized in trap-neuter-return programs in the USA
authors: Dalrymple AM, MacDonald LJ, Kreisler RE
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
citation: Dalrymple AM, MacDonald LJ, Kreisler RE Ear-tipping practices for identification of cats sterilized in trap-neuter-return programs in the USA. Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery. 2022. doi:10.1177/1098612X221105843
abstract: This study examined ear-tipping practices used in trap-neuter-return (TNR) programs across the USA. The researchers distributed an anonymous survey to 526 TNR program participants between October 4-20, 2021, with 410 completing it. Results showed that nearly all respondents recognized the ear tip as indicating sterilization, though some associated it with rabies vaccination or socialization status. Most practitioners tipped the left ear (81%) using visual estimation (92%), preferring a straight-across silhouette. The median post-hemostasis bleeding rate was 5%, with median negative feedback at 1%. The most common complaint involved removing excessive ear tissue. The study found significant variation in techniques without clear superior methods, concluding that standards for this procedure would be helpful.

mcqs.q: A US survey of TNR program participants found that nearly all recognized the ear tip as indicating sterilization, but a minority associated it with rabies vaccination or socialization status. What is the programmatic implication?
o: Because most practitioners correctly interpret the ear tip, no standardization of its meaning is needed

Inconsistent interpretation of the ear tip's meaning among a minority of practitioners can lead to unnecessary recapture or anesthesia of already-sterilized cats, highlighting the value of clear universal education on ear tip significance
The ear tip should be replaced with microchip-only identification to eliminate ambiguity
TNR programs should add secondary markers (tattoos, tags) because the ear tip alone is unreliable as an identifier
mcqs.e: Although the vast majority recognized the ear tip as indicating sterilization, minority interpretations (rabies vaccination, socialization) risk unnecessary recapture or surgery. Standardized education across TNR programs can reduce this risk.

mcqs.q: The 2022 US ear tipping survey found significant variation in techniques with no clearly superior method identified. What practical conclusion follows for the field?
o: Each practitioner should continue using whatever technique they were trained in, as outcomes are equivalent
Without a clearly superior technique, the field would benefit from agreed-upon standards to reduce unwarranted variation and support quality assurance across programs
Ear tipping should be standardized by mandating a single technique nationally to eliminate variation
Technique variation is desirable because it allows practitioners to optimize for local conditions
mcqs.e: The authors explicitly concluded that technique standards would be helpful. High variation without a clear superiority winner means programs lack guidance; standards can reduce unwarranted variation and improve consistency without necessarily mandating a single technique.

title: Characteristics of cat semi-owners
authors: Ma GC, McLeod LJ, Zito SJ
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
citation: Ma GC, McLeod LJ, Zito SJ Characteristics of cat semi-owners. Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery. 2023. doi:10.1177/1098612X231194225
abstract: The study examined people who care for stray cats without considering themselves owners. Researchers surveyed 8,708 New South Wales residents, finding that 588 respondents (7%) were 'semi-owners' of unowned cats. These individuals were significantly more likely to be female, urban-dwelling, from lower socioeconomic areas, and renting their homes. Notably, most semi-owners also owned their own cats and had more cats than non-semi-owners. The researchers concluded that semi-owners represent an important target audience for behavior change interventions aimed at managing cat populations, but interventions must acknowledge barriers like cost and trust issues.

mcqs.q: A survey of New South Wales residents found that 7% were 'semi-owners'—people who fed stray cats without considering themselves owners—and these individuals were more likely to be female, urban, lower socioeconomic status, and renters. What does this profile suggest for designing community cat programs?
o: Semi-owners should be required to formally adopt the cats they feed, converting them to full legal owners with corresponding responsibilities

Community cat programs should be designed with accessibility in mind: semi-owners face cost and housing barriers, so programs offering free or low-cost sterilization and desexing support are likely to have the most impact on this key population
Since semi-owners already own other cats, they have adequate resources and do not need targeted support from cat management programs
Urban semi-owners are more compliant with regulations than rural semi-owners and should be prioritized for TNR outreach
mcqs.e: Semi-owners from lower socioeconomic areas and rental housing face financial and regulatory barriers (e.g., pet restrictions in rental leases). Cost-accessible programs and trust-building outreach are critical to engage this population in cat population management.

mcqs.q: The NSW semi-owner study found that most semi-owners also owned their own cats and had more total cats than non-semi-owners. What does this suggest about semi-owners as a leverage point for cat population management?
o: Semi-owners should be excluded from cat population programs because their high cat numbers indicate they contribute to overpopulation

Semi-owners are already engaged with multiple cats and represent a high-contact population; effectively reaching them with sterilization messaging and services could prevent significant reproduction across both owned and unowned cats in their care
Because semi-owners already own sterilized pets, their unowned cats are likely already sterilized through cross-exposure
Semi-owners are less interested in sterilization than traditional owners because they do not identify as owners
mcqs.e: Semi-owners interact with more cats than non-semi-owners (owned plus unowned), making them a high-leverage contact for sterilization programs. Engaging them effectively—acknowledging barriers of cost and trust—could reduce reproduction across a larger cat cohort than programs targeting formal pet owners alone.

title: Feline chaphamaparvovirus (feline fechavirus) in different cat populations
authors: Weese JS, MacNicol J
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
citation: Weese JS, MacNicol J Feline chaphamaparvovirus (feline fechavirus) in different cat populations. Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery. 2026. doi:10.1177/1098612X261428723
abstract: The researchers assessed the presence of feline chaphamaparvovirus (FeChPV) across various feline populations. They gathered fecal and vomitus samples from 136 cats across multiple facilities: 65 from a shelter without apparent gastrointestinal disease, 25 from shelters experiencing vomiting/diarrhea clusters, and 46 from a research colony following a recent outbreak. Testing revealed FeChPV in 30 of 136 samples (22%). Infection rates varied by location: 12% in the asymptomatic shelter, 11-25% in affected shelters, and 88% in one shelter with acute disease. Notably, the virus appeared in both symptomatic cats (33% of diarrheic animals) and healthy ones (17% of non-symptomatic cats). The researchers concluded that while FeChPV correlates with facility outbreaks, its precise pathogenic role remains ambiguous since detection occurred in healthy populations.

mcqs.q: Feline chaphamaparvovirus (FeChPV) was detected in both symptomatic and healthy shelter cats. What does this mean for outbreak attribution?
o: FeChPV is a confirmed primary pathogen responsible for all shelter GI outbreaks and should be tested for routinely
FeChPV detection in a shelter GI outbreak does not confirm causality because the virus is also found in clinically healthy cats
FeChPV has no association with shelter outbreaks and is an incidental finding
A high FeChPV detection rate in a shelter definitively identifies it as the outbreak cause and justifies isolation measures
mcqs.e: FeChPV was detected in both symptomatic (33% of diarrheic cats) and healthy cats (17% asymptomatic), and detection rates varied widely across facilities (12–88%). Its pathogenic role is ambiguous; detection alone does not confirm causality in an outbreak, and a test-positive result should not end investigation of other pathogens.

mcqs.q: What is the current understanding of feline chaphamaparvovirus (FeChPV) as a shelter pathogen?
o: FeChPV is a well-characterized primary pathogen with a validated treatment protocol
FeChPV correlates with some shelter GI outbreaks but its precise pathogenic role remains ambiguous
FeChPV is not detected in symptomatic cats and is considered a commensal virus
FeChPV has been shown to be more pathogenic than FPV in kittens under 6 weeks of age
mcqs.e: FeChPV correlates with facility outbreaks — particularly high rates (88%) were seen in one shelter during an acute disease event — but detection also occurs in asymptomatic cats. Its precise pathogenic role remains ambiguous, meaning it warrants awareness and investigation but is not yet a definitive outbreak marker.

title: Effects of intranasal maropitant on clinical signs of naturally acquired upper respiratory disease in shelter cats
authors: Parncutt J, Johnson LR, Subharat S, Oke B, Hill KE
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
citation: Parncutt J, Johnson LR, Subharat S, Oke B, Hill KE Effects of intranasal maropitant on clinical signs of naturally acquired upper respiratory disease in shelter cats. Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery. 2025. doi:10.1177/1098612X241309826
abstract: The research team investigated whether intranasal maropitant citrate could reduce severity of feline upper respiratory disease (FURD) in shelter settings. Sixty-one cats received either intranasal maropitant (34 cats) or saline placebo (27 cats) twice daily for seven days. Clinical assessments measured conjunctivitis, blepharospasm, ocular discharge, and nasal discharge using visual analogue scales at baseline and completion. Key finding: there was no significant difference in clinical index scores between the maropitant treatment and control groups for conjunctivitis, blepharospasm, ocular discharge, nasal discharge or total disease severity after 7 days. The researchers concluded that intranasal maropitant showed no clinical benefit compared to saline treatment, and found no evidence to support the routine use of intranasal maropitant in managing feline upper respiratory disease.

mcqs.q: Intranasal maropitant was evaluated as a treatment for feline upper respiratory disease in shelter cats. What was the conclusion?
o: Intranasal maropitant significantly reduced ocular discharge and nasal discharge scores compared to placebo
Intranasal maropitant showed no clinical benefit compared to saline and should not be used routinely for feline URD
Intranasal maropitant reduced conjunctivitis but had no effect on nasal disease
Intranasal maropitant was beneficial in cats with mild disease but not in those with severe signs
mcqs.e: There was no significant difference in any clinical outcome (conjunctivitis, blepharospasm, ocular discharge, nasal discharge, total disease severity) between maropitant and saline after 7 days. There is no evidence to support routine intranasal maropitant use for feline upper respiratory disease in shelters.

mcqs.q: A shelter clinician proposes using intranasal maropitant to reduce the severity and duration of feline URD in cats awaiting adoption. What does current evidence support?
o: This is a well-supported intervention — intranasal maropitant reduces both severity and duration of feline URD
The evidence does not support this use — clinical trial data showed no benefit over saline placebo
Evidence supports a benefit for nasal signs but not ocular signs, so partial use is justified
Intranasal maropitant is effective but only when combined with systemic doxycycline
mcqs.e: A randomized controlled trial found no significant difference between intranasal maropitant and saline placebo on any measured clinical parameter after 7 days of twice-daily administration. This direct clinical trial evidence does not support incorporating intranasal maropitant into shelter URD management protocols.

title: Randomized, non-inferiority clinical trial of three topical dermatophytosis treatments in shelter cats
authors: DeTar L, Janke KJ, Jacobson L
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
citation: DeTar L, Janke KJ, Jacobson L Randomized, non-inferiority clinical trial of three topical dermatophytosis treatments in shelter cats. Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery. 2025. doi:10.1177/1098612X251360611
abstract: This prospective randomized trial evaluated three topical antifungal treatments for cats with Microsporum canis infections in shelter settings. All cats received oral itraconazole while being assigned to one of three topical groups: lime sulfur (LS), miconazole chlorhexidine (MC), or hydrogen peroxide (HP) shampoo. The study enrolled 76 cats across four US shelters. Lime sulfur significantly outperformed alternatives, achieving mycological cure by 7 weeks in all treated cats, compared to 62.5% of MC-treated and 78.3% of HP-treated cats. Mean time to cure was 27 days for LS versus 37 days for MC and 36 days for HP. Younger cats required longer treatment periods. Staff noted no meaningful differences between products regarding application difficulty or feline tolerance, though some side effects were documented including bleached hair (HP) and hypothermia (MC and HP). The researchers concluded that while LS demonstrated superior efficacy, hydrogen peroxide represents an acceptable alternative to lime sulfur if preferred.

mcqs.q: A randomized trial compared lime sulfur (LS), miconazole-chlorhexidine (MC), and hydrogen peroxide (HP) as topical treatments alongside oral itraconazole for shelter cats with Microsporum canis dermatophytosis. What was the hierarchy of efficacy?
o: All three products achieved equivalent cure rates by 7 weeks, with no statistically significant differences
Lime sulfur achieved mycological cure in all cats by 7 weeks, significantly outperforming MC (62.5%) and HP (78.3%)
Hydrogen peroxide was superior to lime sulfur and is now the recommended first-line topical agent
Miconazole-chlorhexidine was most effective but was poorly tolerated by cats and staff
mcqs.e: Lime sulfur achieved 100% mycological cure by 7 weeks versus 62.5% (MC) and 78.3% (HP), with a mean time to cure of 27 days versus 37 and 36 days respectively. LS is the superior topical agent, though HP is an acceptable alternative when LS is not preferred.

mcqs.q: When choosing a topical treatment for shelter dermatophytosis alongside systemic itraconazole, which statement about lime sulfur and hydrogen peroxide is most accurate?
