o: Hydrogen peroxide is preferred over lime sulfur because it has superior efficacy and no relevant side effects
Lime sulfur is the most efficacious option, but hydrogen peroxide represents an acceptable alternative when lime sulfur is not preferred
Both products have identical cure rates, so clinical preference and cost should drive selection
Neither lime sulfur nor hydrogen peroxide should be used alongside itraconazole due to interaction risks
mcqs.e: Lime sulfur achieved superior cure rates, but the study authors conclude HP is an acceptable alternative. Both products had documented side effects (bleached hair for HP; hypothermia with MC and HP). Staff noted no meaningful differences in application difficulty or feline tolerance between products.

title: The effect of animal shelter sound on cat behaviour and welfare
authors: Eagan BH, Gordon E, Fraser D
journal: Animal Welfare
citation: Eagan BH, Gordon E, Fraser D The effect of animal shelter sound on cat behaviour and welfare. Animal Welfare. 2021. doi:10.7120/09627286.30.4.006
abstract: This investigation assessed how sound affected fearand maintenance-related behaviors in single-housed shelter cats. Two daily 30-minute observation sessions (morning and evening) occurred for 98 cats over ten days. Cat behaviour and presence of sound (classified by source) were recorded by instantaneous and one-zero sampling with 15-second intervals. Sessions were classified as 'quiet' or 'noisy' based on median sound levels. Statistical analysis included 70 cats with adequate comparable observations. Males demonstrated less fear and maintenance behavior than females. Morning sessions consistently had much more sound than evenings, and cats showed more fear behaviour and less maintenance behaviour in the mornings. Cats exhibited more fear responses during noisy morning sessions compared to quiet ones. When sound transitioned from quiet to noisy, fear-related behaviour increased; transitions from noisy to quiet showed decreased fear behaviours. The findings indicate that shelter cats vary significantly in responsiveness, and environmental sound substantially influences their conduct. The researchers conclude that reducing shelter noise levels may enhance overall welfare outcomes for cats.

mcqs.q: A study of 98 shelter cats found that noisy conditions were associated with increased fear behavior and decreased maintenance behavior. What is the most actionable welfare recommendation from these findings?
o: Rotate cats between noisy and quiet areas to promote desensitization
Administer anxiolytics during morning cleaning periods when sound peaks
Reduce shelter noise levels as a practical strategy to improve cat welfare
House cats and dogs in adjacent areas to acclimate cats to environmental sound
mcqs.e: The researchers explicitly conclude that reducing shelter noise levels may enhance overall welfare outcomes for cats. Sound was modifiable and directly linked to fear behavior — making noise reduction the most direct and practical intervention.

mcqs.q: In this shelter sound study, morning sessions had significantly more sound than evenings, and cats showed more fear behavior in the mornings. What does this pattern suggest about noise management?
o: Fear behavior is driven by circadian rhythms, not sound — morning cleaning should proceed normally
Noise during morning routines (cleaning, feeding) is a modifiable welfare risk that warrants targeted reduction strategies
Evening sessions should be restructured to match morning sound levels for consistency
The morning–evening pattern shows cats habituate to sound quickly and no intervention is needed
mcqs.e: Morning sessions had more sound AND more fear behavior; when sound decreased (evening or quiet transitions), fear decreased. Since morning noise comes largely from human activity, targeted noise reduction strategies during morning routines are a practical welfare intervention.

mcqs.q: Male cats in this shelter sound study showed less fear and maintenance behavior than females. What is the correct interpretation of this finding for shelter practice?
o: Male cats should be housed in noisier areas since they are less sensitive to sound
Female cats should receive anxiolytics prophylactically due to universal higher sensitivity
Individual variation in sound sensitivity exists by sex; a one-size approach to noise management may not be sufficient for all cats
Sex is the primary predictor of fear behavior and should override housing location decisions
mcqs.e: Sex differences in fear and maintenance behavior highlight that shelter cats vary significantly in responsiveness to sound — a finding the authors explicitly note. This supports individualized welfare monitoring rather than uniform protocols based on aggregate data.

title: Animal sheltering: A scoping literature review grounded in institutional ethnography
authors: Koralesky KE, Rankin JM, Fraser D
journal: Animal Welfare
citation: Koralesky KE, Rankin JM, Fraser D Animal sheltering: A scoping literature review grounded in institutional ethnography. Animal Welfare. 2023. doi:10.1017/awf.2022.4
abstract: The authors examined research on animal sheltering through an institutional ethnography lens, focusing on actual work practices. They reviewed literature on three main areas: shelter staff experiences, animal relinquishment, and length of stay in shelters. Key findings reveal that euthanasia-related stress dominates research on staff, yet focus group participants emphasized decision-making tensions rather than the act itself. Research on relinquishment relies heavily on surveys and database records with significant limitations. Length of stay studies focus on animal characteristics like breed and color, overlooking actual work processes like veterinary treatment and behavioral modification. The authors conclude that institutional ethnography offers valuable insights by examining concrete work activities that current quantitative approaches overlook, potentially leading to better support for both animals and staff.

mcqs.q: According to a scoping review using an institutional ethnography lens, what aspect of euthanasia most burdens shelter staff, according to their own focus group accounts?
o: The physical act of administering euthanasia is the primary source of distress
Decision-making tensions around when and whether to euthanize — not the act itself — dominate staff experience
Post-euthanasia grief and lack of bereavement support are the primary stressors
Public criticism of euthanasia decisions on social media is the main driver of staff burnout
mcqs.e: While much of the published research on shelter staff focuses on euthanasia-related stress, focus group participants in this review emphasized decision-making tensions — the dilemmas around when, whether, and how decisions to euthanize are made — as the dominant source of stress rather than the physical act itself. This distinction has important implications for staff support programs, which should address decision-making processes and moral distress, not just emotional aftermath.

mcqs.q: What methodological gap does the institutional ethnography framework identify in existing shelter research on length of stay?
o: Length of stay studies rely too heavily on qualitative interviews, which introduce recall bias
Studies focus on animal characteristics like breed and color, while overlooking work processes such as veterinary treatment and behavioral modification that actually determine how long animals stay
Most length of stay research uses inadequate statistical methods and cannot identify true predictors
Studies over-focus on cats and lack comparable data for dogs and rabbits
mcqs.e: The review found that length of stay research disproportionately examines animal characteristics (breed, coat color) while overlooking the concrete work activities that shape an animal's timeline — including veterinary treatment, behavioral modification, and staff decision-making processes. Institutional ethnography focuses on actual work practices, revealing that these invisible processes are at least as important as animal traits in determining shelter outcomes.

title: Using institutional ethnography to analyse animal sheltering and protection I: Animal protection work
authors: Koralesky KE, Rankin JM, Fraser D
journal: Animal Welfare
citation: Koralesky KE, Rankin JM, Fraser D Using institutional ethnography to analyse animal sheltering and protection I: Animal protection work. Animal Welfare. 2023. doi:10.1017/awf.2023.39
abstract: Animal protection enforcement in Canada relies on citizens reporting concerns, yet the actual work processes of law enforcement have received minimal scholarly attention. This study employed institutional ethnography to examine the daily activities of call centre operators and animal protection officers. The research revealed that staff attempt to identify evidence of animal 'distress' as legally defined, though many cases—such as animals in isolated or deprived situations—fall short of this definition, preventing intervention. Officers face constraints from privacy and property law requirements, and must document compliance attempts to justify further action including search warrants. These limitations can delay or prevent beneficial intervention. Officers sometimes work creatively to advocate for animals when legal tools prove insufficient. The study recommends expanding the legal definition of distress to better address animals' needs, developing broader intervention options for officers, and conducting ethnographic research across jurisdictions with different legal frameworks to understand how laws and policies organize animal protection work.

mcqs.q: Animal protection officers (APOs) in Canada were found to face significant constraints in investigating cruelty/neglect complaints. The most commonly cited legal barrier was:
o: Lack of veterinary expertise to assess animal conditions in the field
Many cases did not meet the legal definition of 'distress,' limiting intervention authority
Privacy law prevented APOs from contacting neighbors for witness statements
Animals' status as property only applied to livestock, not companion animals
mcqs.e: Qualitative findings showed that a substantial proportion of investigated cases did not legally qualify as 'distress' under existing animal welfare law, preventing APOs from taking enforcement action even when animals were in suboptimal conditions.

mcqs.q: An institutional ethnography of animal protection work in Canada concluded that expanding the legal definition of 'distress' would:
o: Increase administrative burden without meaningful welfare improvement
Create liability for APOs who intervene in ambiguous cases
Allow earlier and broader intervention in cases that cause animal suffering but do not currently meet the legal threshold
Primarily benefit commercial breeding facilities rather than companion animals
mcqs.e: The study's recommendation to expand the definition of 'distress' was specifically aimed at closing the gap between observable animal suffering and legal enforceability — enabling APOs to intervene in more cases where welfare is compromised.

title: Using institutional ethnography to analyse animal sheltering and protection II: Animal shelter work
authors: Koralesky KE, Rankin JM, Fraser D
journal: Animal Welfare
citation: Koralesky KE, Rankin JM, Fraser D Using institutional ethnography to analyse animal sheltering and protection II: Animal shelter work. Animal Welfare. 2023. doi:10.1017/awf.2023.83
abstract: The study employed institutional ethnography to examine how frontline shelter staff's daily activities connect to standardized organizational procedures at a large animal protection organization. Staff regularly perform behavioral assessments and review intake documents to guide animal care and inform potential adopters while safeguarding volunteers and the public. However, staff faced significant time constraints and pressure when working with behaviorally challenged animals because their efforts were primarily directed toward facilitating quick adoptions for most animals and preparing for future kennel space demands. Management systems focused on maintaining manageable animal populations based on available resources, reducing shelter duration, and individualized housing. These systems ultimately limited staff's capacity to provide intensive behavioral work for long-stay animals with serious problems. This situation created occupational stress for caregiving staff who felt emotionally invested in these animals' outcomes. The researchers recommend exploring behavioral modification support and expanding foster programs for animals with specialized needs.

mcqs.q: An institutional ethnography of shelter work found that management data systems focused on throughput and LOS metrics created a specific problem for frontline staff. What was that problem?
o: Staff were unable to track which animals had received vaccinations
Population-level metrics reduced capacity for intensive behavioral work with long-stay animals, creating occupational stress
LOS tracking led to premature euthanasia decisions for healthy animals
Throughput pressure caused staff to skip medical intake assessments
mcqs.e: The emphasis on throughput and population metrics created a tension: individual animals needing intensive behavioral support were deprioritized by systems designed to move animals quickly. This mismatch was a source of moral distress and burnout among frontline staff.

mcqs.q: Based on ethnographic findings about shelter work pressures, which intervention is most directly supported by the evidence to reduce staff moral distress?
o: Increasing adoption marketing budgets to improve throughput
Reducing shelter capacity to lower workload
Expanding behavioral modification support and foster programs to reduce tension between throughput pressure and animal welfare
Eliminating LOS tracking to reduce performance pressure on staff
mcqs.e: The study's specific recommendation was to expand behavioral support and foster programs — addressing the root cause of the tension (individual animals needing more time/resources than throughput-focused systems allow), not just the symptoms.

title: Predictors of successful diversion of cats and dogs away from animal shelter intake: Analysis of data from a self-rehoming website
authors: Ly LH, Protopopova A
journal: Animal Welfare
citation: Ly LH, Protopopova A Predictors of successful diversion of cats and dogs away from animal shelter intake: Analysis of data from a self-rehoming website. Animal Welfare. 2023. doi:10.1017/awf.2023.8
abstract: As animals experience distress in animal shelters, leaders call for increased efforts to divert intake of companion animals away from shelters. One novel intake diversion strategy is supported self-rehoming, where owners find new homes for their animals without surrendering to a physical shelter. This study aimed to identify predictors of successful diversion of animals through the AdoptaPet.com 'Rehome' online platform. Data for dogs (n=100,342) and cats (n=48,484) were analysed through logistic regression to assess the association of animaland owner-related factors and outcome. Overall, 87.1% of dogs and 85.7% of cats were successfully diverted from animal shelters, out of which, 37.8% of dogs and 35.3% of cats were kept by their original owner. Multiple animal-related factors predicted increased odds of diversion (e.g. younger, smaller). Dog and cat owners who set a longer rehoming deadline (i.e. >8 weeks) were over twice as likely to keep or adopt out their animal. Dog owners who surrendered for owner-related reasons had increased odds of diversion in comparison to animal behaviour issues. We conclude that online-supported, self-rehoming platforms provide pet owners with an alternative to relinquishment that may reduce the intake of animals to shelters; however, owners with animals that are not preferred by adopters may have to decide whether to keep their animal or relinquish their animal to a shelter or rescue.

mcqs.q: An analysis of over 148,000 AdoptaPet.com 'Rehome' listings found that setting a rehoming deadline of more than 8 weeks was associated with more than double the odds of keeping or rehoming the animal. What is the practical implication for shelter diversion counseling?
o: Owners should be discouraged from setting any deadlines, as pressure increases the likelihood of shelter surrender

Encouraging owners to give themselves at least 8 weeks to find a new home—rather than making an immediate surrender decision—significantly increases the chance of successful diversion from shelter intake
Rehoming deadlines only benefit dog owners; cat owners should be advised to surrender immediately if rehoming seems difficult
The 8-week threshold is specific to the AdoptaPet platform and cannot be applied to other diversion contexts
mcqs.e: Owners who set a deadline greater than 8 weeks had over twice the odds of diversion success. Shelter intake counselors should encourage owners considering surrender to pursue supported self-rehoming with an extended timeframe before making a final surrender decision.

mcqs.q: The self-rehoming platform study found that approximately 87% of dogs and 86% of cats were successfully diverted from shelters, but animals 'not preferred by adopters' (e.g., older, larger, less photogenic) were at risk of remaining with owners who may ultimately surrender them to a shelter. What does this mean for intake diversion programs?
o: Self-rehoming platforms are sufficient for all animals; shelter intake counselors only need to direct owners to the platform

Self-rehoming platforms work well for most animals but have a systematic gap for 'hard to place' animals; diversion programs should pair platform referrals with additional support (e.g., rescue network connections, behavior coaching) for these cases
Animals not preferred by adopters should be surrendered directly to the shelter because self-rehoming will not work for them
Diversion success rates of 85%+ are artificially high because only outcomes favorable to the platform are reported
mcqs.e: The study identified that less-preferred animals risk remaining in limbo with owners who cannot find a new home. For these animals, platform referral alone is insufficient; programs should provide additional support to avoid eventual shelter surrender.

mcqs.q: In the self-rehoming study, dog owners surrendering for owner-related reasons (e.g., moving, allergies) had better diversion outcomes than those surrendering for animal behaviour issues. What does this suggest about intake assessment priorities?
o: Behaviour-related surrender cases should be referred directly to shelters because self-rehoming will not work for them

Intake assessment should distinguish between owner-related and behaviour-related surrender reasons, as the latter predicts lower diversion success and may warrant targeted behaviour support or rescue referral to maximize diversion potential
Owner-related and behaviour-related surrender cases have equivalent diversion outcomes when given sufficient time
Only medically complex cases require differentiated intake assessment; all behaviour cases can use the same diversion pathway
mcqs.e: Behaviour-related surrender was associated with lower diversion odds. This suggests that behavior support services (training referrals, behaviour helplines) alongside self-rehoming platform access could address the root cause and improve diversion rates for this subgroup.

title: Companion animal adoption and relinquishment during the COVID-19 pandemic: The experiences of animal rescue staff and volunteers
authors: Carroll GA, Reeve C, Torjussen A
journal: Animal Welfare
citation: Carroll GA, Reeve C, Torjussen A Companion animal adoption and relinquishment during the COVID-19 pandemic: The experiences of animal rescue staff and volunteers. Animal Welfare. 2024. doi:10.1017/awf.2024.15
abstract: There has been a paucity of research into the experiences of animal rescue staff and volunteers during COVID-19. The aim of this qualitative research was to explore the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on companion animal rescue organisations and their staff and volunteers, and to develop a set of recommendations on how to reduce the risk to companion animal welfare during a crisis. Descriptive thematic analysis was used to explore the experiences of staff and volunteers from 28 animal rescue organisations, most of which were based in the UK. Other surveyed countries included Germany, the Republic of Ireland, France, Spain, the USA and Australia. We identify three key themes that reflect the challenges faced by pet rescue organisations during the pandemic: (1) impact on animals; (2) impact on identity; and (3) impact on organisational processes. Key recommendations include the promotion of co-operation and modifications within the sector, the need to understand, and change, detrimental pet-owner behaviours, and the need to clarify the identity of animal rescue organisations within the Government. Both positive and negative outcomes were experienced by animal rescue organisations during the COVID-19 pandemic. These findings should be considered for future crises and indeed the everyday operating procedures of companion animal rescue organisations.

mcqs.q: Qualitative research with animal rescue staff and volunteers across multiple countries during COVID-19 identified what as a key recommendation for crisis preparedness?
o: Rescue organizations should operate independently during crises to avoid conflicting government guidance
Increased co-operation within the sector and clarification of rescue organizations' identity within government structures are needed
Online adoption should replace all in-person adoption events during any future public health emergency
Rescue workers should be classified as emergency services to ensure operational continuity during pandemics
mcqs.e: The study identified three key themes: impact on animals, impact on identity, and impact on organisational processes. Key recommendations included promoting sector co-operation, addressing detrimental pet-owner behaviours, and clarifying the identity of animal rescue organisations within government — especially relevant for future crisis planning.

mcqs.q: Animal rescue organizations reported both positive and negative outcomes during the COVID-19 pandemic. Which challenge most affected organizational sustainability and animal welfare in rescue settings?
o: Inability to conduct international rescue transports due to border closures
Disruption to organisational identity and processes, alongside increased demand and operational constraints
Legislative changes that permanently restricted rescue operations in most surveyed countries
Lack of any adoption demand during lockdown periods, leading to severe overcrowding
mcqs.e: The study identified disruption to organisational identity (e.g., uncertainty about rescue's role) and organisational process challenges as key themes, alongside impact on the animals themselves. These findings have implications for how shelters and rescues prepare crisis communication and operational contingency plans.

title: Companion animal adoption and relinquishment during the COVID-19 pandemic: Households with children at greatest risk of relinquishing a cat or dog
authors: Carroll GA, Torjussen A, Reeve C
journal: Animal Welfare
citation: Carroll GA, Torjussen A, Reeve C Companion animal adoption and relinquishment during the COVID-19 pandemic: Households with children at greatest risk of relinquishing a cat or dog. Animal Welfare. 2023. doi:10.1017/awf.2023.77
abstract: The study examined factors linked to pet relinquishment during COVID-19 across multiple countries. Researchers surveyed 3,945 pet owners and identified that households with children were 4.6 times more likely to consider or have already relinquished a cat or dog compared to those without children. Additional risk factors included male pet ownership and younger animal age. Notably, the analysis found no association between online acquisition source and relinquishment risk. Among those who relinquished pets, 76.2% found the decision emotionally difficult, though all agreed it was logically correct. The USA showed significantly higher relinquishment rates than the UK and Italy. The research highlights the need for targeted interventions supporting families with children in pet retention.

mcqs.q: During the COVID-19 pandemic, which household characteristic was most strongly associated with risk of pet relinquishment?
o: Male pet ownership and online acquisition of the pet
Younger animal age and acquisition from a breeder
Having children in the household, with an approximately 4.6-fold increased risk
Geographic location, with urban households at highest risk
mcqs.e: Households with children were 4.6 times more likely to consider or have already relinquished a cat or dog. Additional risk factors included male pet ownership and younger animal age. Online acquisition source was not associated with relinquishment risk.

mcqs.q: For shelter relinquishment prevention programs, what does pandemic-era data most strongly suggest about targeting interventions?
o: Interventions should focus on senior pet owners because elderly households have the most difficulty providing care during crises
Families with children should be a priority target for retention support, as they face substantially higher relinquishment risk
Online-sourced pet owners should be prioritized because they lack established relationships with veterinary care
All demographic groups face equal relinquishment risk, so universal outreach is more effective than targeted programs
mcqs.e: Households with children were at 4.6-fold higher relinquishment risk — by far the strongest single predictor identified. Targeted interventions supporting families with children in pet retention (e.g., flexible rehoming alternatives, emergency boarding, financial assistance) are most likely to be efficient.

title: Shelter and rescue programmes associated with higher live release and lower return rates for dogs
authors: Reese LA
journal: Animal Welfare
citation: Reese LA Shelter and rescue programmes associated with higher live release and lower return rates for dogs. Animal Welfare. 2021. doi:10.7120/09627286.30.4.005
abstract: The research examines how shelter characteristics and initiatives affect positive outcomes for dogs. Drawing on survey data from 370 U.S. animal shelters and rescues, the study identifies three key factors associated with improved results: avoiding breed designations for mixed-breed dogs, maintaining robust foster networks, and implementing matching systems. The findings indicate that it is the programmes shelters and rescues implement, not simply their human and financial resources, that are associated with positive outcomes.

mcqs.q: A survey of 370 U.S. shelters and rescues examined what drives better live release and lower return rates. Which three programme factors were most associated with positive outcomes?
o: Larger budgets, more staff per animal, and newer facilities
Avoiding breed designations for mixed-breed dogs, maintaining robust foster networks, and using matching systems
Requiring pre-adoption home visits, mandatory training classes, and post-adoption follow-up calls
Marketing spend, social media presence, and partnership with national adoption platforms
mcqs.e: The study found that outcomes were driven by the programmes shelters implement — not simply their resources. The three key factors were avoiding breed labels for mixed-breed dogs, strong foster networks, and matching systems.

mcqs.q: The finding that outcomes are associated with programmes rather than resources has what implication for smaller or lower-resourced shelters?
o: Smaller shelters should focus only on reducing intake until they secure more funding
Low-resource shelters can improve outcomes by adopting evidence-based programme practices without necessarily increasing their budget
This finding only applies to large rescues with existing digital infrastructure
Resources are the true driver and the programme finding is a statistical artefact
mcqs.e: The key conclusion is that it is what shelters do — not just what they have — that improves outcomes. This means programme changes (e.g., removing breed labels, building a foster network) are accessible levers for organisations of any size.

title: The role of breed and personality descriptions in influencing perceptions of shelter dog adoptability
authors: Archer C, Hall NJ, Andrukonis A
journal: Animal Welfare
citation: Archer C, Hall NJ, Andrukonis A The role of breed and personality descriptions in influencing perceptions of shelter dog adoptability. Animal Welfare. 2025. doi:10.1017/awf.2025.10043
abstract: The study examined how breed labels and personality descriptions affect potential adopters' likelihood of choosing shelter dogs. Researchers presented dog photographs to participants under four conditions: photo alone, photo with breed identification, photo with personality traits, and photo with both elements combined. Key findings indicate that descriptions significantly increased perceived adoptability, while breed labels decreased it. Specific breed designations like Chihuahua mix, Chow mix, and Jack Russell Terrier mix negatively influenced adoption interest, whereas 'Lab mix' improved ratings. Personality descriptors such as affectionate, calm, and friendly boosted perceived adoptability; notably, 'energetic' reduced adoption interest. The research suggests removing breed labels and incorporating positive personality descriptions could enhance adoption outcomes and potentially reduce how long dogs remain in shelters, thereby supporting animal welfare objectives.

mcqs.q: When potential adopters viewed shelter dog photos accompanied by breed labels versus personality descriptions, which had a positive effect on perceived adoptability?
o: Breed labels increased adoptability ratings while personality descriptions had no effect
Both breed labels and personality descriptions equally increased adoption interest
Personality descriptions increased perceived adoptability while breed labels decreased it
Neither breed labels nor personality descriptions significantly affected adoption interest
mcqs.e: Personality descriptions (e.g., affectionate, calm, friendly) significantly increased perceived adoptability, while breed labels — including Chihuahua mix, Chow mix, Jack Russell Terrier mix — decreased it. Only 'Lab mix' improved ratings among breed labels.

mcqs.q: What is the most directly actionable shelter practice recommended by this research?
o: Conduct DNA testing on all dogs to provide accurate breed information for adopters
Remove breed labels from adoption listings and replace them with positive personality descriptions to increase adoption interest
List only dogs with 'Lab mix' heritage to maximise adoption rates
Use breed labels only for purebred dogs and omit them for mixed breeds
mcqs.e: The evidence directly supports removing potentially stigmatising breed labels and instead leading with personality descriptors. This change is low-cost, immediately implementable, and supported by the study's finding that descriptions increase and breed labels decrease adoption interest.

title: Shelter Worker's Experiences and Perceptions of Capacity for Care (C4C)
authors: Hobson S, Bateman S, Coe JB, Oblak ML
journal: Journal of Applied Animal Welfare Science
citation: Hobson S, Bateman S, Coe JB, Oblak ML Shelter Worker's Experiences and Perceptions of Capacity for Care (C4C). Journal of Applied Animal Welfare Science. 2023. doi:10.1080/10888705.2021.1910033
abstract: Capacity for Care (C4C) is a shelter population management strategy which utilizes managed intake to optimize in-shelter populations based on housing capacity and available resources. The purpose of this study was to (1) understand staff experiences using managed intake, (2) explore staff perceptions of how the C4C model has been regarded by other staff at their facility, and (3) explore the response of community members who are attempting to relinquish their cats, as perceived by the staff who are communicating with cat owners and scheduling relinquishment. Participants recruited from shelters who practiced C4C participated in a semi-structured interview and completed a written survey to share their experiences and perceptions of C4C. Based on the perceptions of the participants, evidence suggests the waitlist may decrease the admission of owned cats to the shelter as a result of advising cat owners about alternatives to relinquishment. Additional investigation would help clarify how managed intake affects community cats awaiting shelter admission.

mcqs.q: A shelter implementing Capacity for Care (C4C) added a waitlist for owned-cat admissions. What was the observed effect on owned-cat intake?
o: Owned-cat intake increased as publicity about the waitlist attracted more surrenders
Owned-cat intake was unchanged; owners waited and eventually surrendered anyway
Owned-cat intake appeared to decrease, as owners were redirected toward community alternatives
Owned-cat intake decreased but community stray intake increased proportionally
mcqs.e: The waitlist appeared to decrease owned-cat intake by redirecting owners toward community alternatives (rehoming, behavioral support, etc.) rather than surrender — a key mechanism by which C4C can reduce admission pressure without simply turning animals away.

mcqs.q: After implementing Capacity for Care, what gap in knowledge was identified regarding its effects?
o: Whether C4C reduces euthanasia rates in owner-relinquished animals
Whether staff perceive C4C as ethical
Whether limiting owned-cat admissions affects community (stray) cat intake
Whether C4C improves animal health outcomes during housing
mcqs.e: While the waitlist appeared to reduce owned-cat intake, the effect on community/stray cat intake was unclear and identified as an evidence gap — an important consideration because diverting one intake stream could shift pressure to another.

title: Community factors and animal shelter outcomes
authors: Reese LA
journal: Journal of Applied Animal Welfare Science
citation: Reese LA Community factors and animal shelter outcomes. Journal of Applied Animal Welfare Science. 2024. doi:10.1080/10888705.2022.2063021
abstract: This research explores connections between the nature of a community, the type of animal shelter it has, how animals arrive at the shelter, and outcomes for the animals in terms of adoption or euthanasia. Based on data from Shelter Animals Count, the study concludes that the nature of the local community is related to the type of shelter it is served by, how dogs arrive at the shelter, and directly to outcomes. Areas with greater economic stress and lower educational attainment are more likely to have a municipal shelter, which increases stray intake, and ultimately euthanasia. Community economic stress is also directly associated with lower adoption and higher euthanasia rates. The findings of the study suggest a multi-pronged strategy to increase adoptions and reduce euthanasia focusing on both animal shelters but also using a One Health approach to improve the welfare of both humans and non-human animals.

mcqs.q: What community-level factor is most strongly associated with higher euthanasia rates in animal shelters?
o: Geographic remoteness and lack of nearby adoption networks
Community economic stress and lower educational attainment, which increase stray intake and reduce adoptions
The proportion of rental versus owned housing in the community
The density of pet-owning households relative to shelter capacity
mcqs.e: Based on Shelter Animals Count data, communities with greater economic stress and lower educational attainment were more likely to have municipal shelters, experience higher stray intake, and have lower adoption and higher euthanasia rates. Economic stress was also directly associated with outcomes, independent of the shelter type. This finding supports a One Health framing: improving human welfare in disadvantaged communities also improves animal welfare outcomes.

mcqs.q: If a shelter wants to reduce euthanasia rates, what does this community-level analysis suggest is insufficient as a standalone strategy?
o: Increasing shelter capacity and staffing
Focusing solely on shelter-based interventions — community economic and educational factors directly influence outcomes, requiring multi-pronged strategies beyond the shelter itself
Implementing TNR programs for community cats
Increasing marketing for adoption events
mcqs.e: The study found that community characteristics — economic stress, educational attainment — are directly associated with shelter intake patterns and outcomes. A shelter-centric approach alone cannot fully address euthanasia rates driven by socioeconomic factors. The authors recommend multi-pronged strategies addressing both shelter operations and broader community welfare, consistent with a One Health approach that links animal and human wellbeing.

title: Attitudes Toward Spay/Neuter in the US Population: Urban/Rural, Cat/Dog, and Demographic Differences
authors: Glasser CL
journal: Anthrozoös
citation: Glasser CL Attitudes Toward Spay/Neuter in the US Population: Urban/Rural, Cat/Dog, and Demographic Differences. Anthrozoös. 2021. doi:10.1080/08927936.2021.1874112
abstract: An online survey of 991 US adults examines differences in attitudes among the general US population toward spaying and neutering cats and dogs, with a focus on differences between urban and rural respondents and the influence of demographic characteristics. Twelve items measure attitudes toward spay/neuter. Each item is analyzed with a separate multiple regression to understand urban–rural, cat–dog and demographic differences in attitudes. Results indicate fewer urban–rural and cat–dog differences than expected, though rural respondents are less likely to find the practice cruel, think animals should have a litter before sterilization, or support laws to require sterilization. People asked about dogs are more likely to agree that spay/neuter operations are expensive but are less likely to believe it is the right thing to do than those asked about cats. The most prevalent characteristics impacting attitudes are guardianship, age, and gender, with guardians more likely to attribute positive health and behavioral outcomes to sterilization and feel that it is morally and socially positive.

mcqs.q: A US survey found fewer urban-rural differences in attitudes toward spay/neuter than expected, but rural respondents were less likely to support mandatory sterilization laws. What is the most important implication for policy advocacy?
o: Urban-rural agreement on core attitudes means national mandatory sterilization legislation would be broadly accepted

Despite general agreement that spay/neuter is beneficial, resistance to mandatory legislation is higher in rural areas, suggesting policy approaches should emphasize access and incentives rather than legal mandates to achieve rural compliance
Rural opposition to mandatory sterilization laws means advocacy efforts in rural areas are futile
Urban respondents oppose mandatory sterilization laws at similar rates to rural respondents, so the policy approach should be uniform
mcqs.e: Rural respondents had lower support for mandatory spay/neuter laws even while sharing many positive attitudes toward the practice. Policies framed around access and voluntary participation are more likely to succeed in rural communities than legally mandated approaches.

mcqs.q: The spay/neuter attitudes survey found that pet guardians (owners) were more likely than non-guardians to attribute positive health and behavioral outcomes to sterilization. What does this imply about how sterilization messaging should be targeted?
o: Messaging should focus on pet owners since non-owners are unlikely to influence sterilization rates

Non-guardian community members are an underutilized audience: because they are less convinced of health and behavioral benefits, outreach that builds their understanding of sterilization's value can shift community norms and reduce stigma
Guardianship is the main barrier to sterilization uptake and should be addressed by reducing pet ownership in low-income areas
Non-guardians hold uniformly negative attitudes toward sterilization and are resistant to evidence-based messaging
mcqs.e: Guardians were more positive about sterilization outcomes than non-guardians. Since non-guardians make up a large share of the community and influence norms, outreach that reaches beyond pet owners—addressing perceived benefits and dispelling myths—can build broader community support for sterilization programs.

title: Temporal trends in intake category data for animal shelter and rescue organizations in Colorado from 2008 to 2018
authors: Hawes SM, Hupe TM, Gandenberger J, Morris KN
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
citation: Hawes SM, Hupe TM, Gandenberger J, Morris KN Temporal trends in intake category data for animal shelter and rescue organizations in Colorado from 2008 to 2018. Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association. 2022. doi:10.2460/javma.20.08.0426
abstract: Objective: To investigate trends in animal shelter and rescue organization intake for dogs and cats in Colorado from 2008 to 2018. Sample: 482 animal shelters and rescue organizations that reported annual intake data to the State of Colorado Department of Agriculture for 1,086,630 dogs and 702,333 cats. Procedures: Total intake, intake for each of 5 Pet Animal Care and Facilities Act (PACFA) categories (stray, owner surrender, intrastate transfer, interstate transfer, or other), and community-based intake (total intake after exclusion of transfers) of dogs and cats were assessed in total and for each organization type (shelter or rescue organization). The number taken in per year, number taken in/1,000 capita, and number in each intake category as a percentage of total intake were analyzed with linear regression models. Results: Trend lines indicated that total dog intake increased over the study period, but there was no change when these data were adjusted for the human population. Additionally, cat intake decreased over time according to both of these measures. For dogs, the stray percentage decreased while the interstate transfer percentage increased over time. Cat stray percentages also decreased while owner surrender percentages increased. Rescue organizations showed the largest increase in dog interstate transfers. Conclusions and Clinical Relevance: Monitoring intake category trends at the state level can help guide resource allocation and policy decisions for both shelters and rescue organizations.

mcqs.q: Analysis of Colorado shelter data from 2008–2018 showed that total dog intake increased, but per-capita dog intake was flat. The most important operational interpretation is:
o: Dog overpopulation problems have been solved and no further intervention is needed
Population growth alone drove the raw intake increase; community dog ownership rates were stable
Per-capita stability means intake prevention programs had no effect
Flat per-capita intake indicates shelters were artificially capping admissions
mcqs.e: Flat per-capita intake alongside rising raw numbers indicates that population growth — not worsening community animal welfare — drove the raw increase. This reframes the problem: the dog shelter burden is growing in absolute terms primarily due to human population growth.

mcqs.q: Between 2008 and 2018 in Colorado, the percentage of dog intake coming from strays DECREASED while the percentage from interstate transfers INCREASED. What does this shift indicate for shelter planning?
o: Stray dog programs are no longer necessary
The source of shelter dogs is shifting from local community strays toward regional/national transport networks, requiring different intake and population management strategies
Interstate transfers have replaced owner surrenders as the dominant intake category
The decrease in stray intake reflects declining community dog ownership
mcqs.e: The compositional shift — fewer local strays, more interstate transfers — means shelters increasingly function as part of a national redistribution system rather than just local animal control. Operational planning and resource allocation must account for this change.

mcqs.q: For cats in Colorado shelters 2008–2018, which trend was observed in owner surrenders as a proportion of total cat intake?
o: Owner surrender percentage decreased as stray intake dominated
Owner surrender percentage was stable throughout the decade
Owner surrender percentage increased, even as overall cat intake declined
Owner surrender percentage decreased due to effective rehoming campaigns
mcqs.e: Total cat intake declined (raw and per capita), and stray intake percentage decreased — but owner surrender percentage increased. This suggests that while stray cat management efforts made gains, owner surrender remained a growing relative concern within a shrinking overall cat intake.

title: Retrospective review reveals few complications of ovarian pedicle tie in 15,927 cats undergoing ovariohysterectomy at a large HQHVSN clinic and training facility in the United States: 2017–2018
authors: Rigdon-Brestle K, Accornero VH, Amtower M, Slater MR
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
citation: Rigdon-Brestle K, Accornero VH, Amtower M, Slater MR Retrospective review reveals few complications of ovarian pedicle tie in 15,927 cats undergoing ovariohysterectomy at a large HQHVSN clinic and training facility in the United States: 2017–2018. Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association. 2022. doi:10.2460/javma.21.09.0405
abstract: Objective: To determine the rate of complications associated with the ovarian pedicle tie procedure in cats undergoing ovariohysterectomy and to examine whether cat characteristics or surgeon experience level were associated with complications. Design: Retrospective cohort study. Animals: 15,927 cats that underwent ovariohysterectomy with the ovarian pedicle tie procedure at a large high-quality, high-volume spay-neuter (HQHVSN) clinic and training facility in the US between January 1, 2017, and December 31, 2018. Procedures: Data were extracted from electronic and paper medical records. Complications examined included pedicle drop or tear, pedicle hemorrhage, and pedicle-related death. Complications were coded by a veterinarian blinded to surgeon experience level. Results: Only 19 of 15,927 (0.12%) cats had pedicle-related hemorrhage, and in all instances, hemorrhage was corrected intraoperatively without serious complication or death. No pedicle-related deaths occurred. Cat reproductive status, body weight, age, and surgeon experience level were not significantly associated with pedicle-related complications. Conclusions and Clinical Relevance: The ovarian pedicle tie is a safe technique for ovariohysterectomy in cats when performed in a HQHVSN setting, with a very low rate of pedicle-related hemorrhage. Surgeon experience level did not significantly affect complication rates, suggesting the technique is learnable across skill levels.

mcqs.q: A retrospective study of 15,927 feline ovariohysterectomies using the ovarian pedicle tie technique at a HQHVSN clinic found a pedicle-related hemorrhage rate of 0.12%, with no deaths. What is the key clinical take-home about this technique?
o: The ovarian pedicle tie should only be performed by senior surgeons because of significant hemorrhage risk
The ovarian pedicle tie is a safe technique for feline OHE in HQHVSN settings, with a very low complication rate that did not vary significantly with surgeon experience level
The 0.12% hemorrhage rate is unacceptably high for elective surgery and argues against using this technique
The low complication rate only applies to cats under 2 kg; larger or older cats are at substantially higher risk
mcqs.e: Only 19 of 15,927 cats had pedicle-related hemorrhage (0.12%), all corrected intraoperatively without death. Crucially, surgeon experience level did not significantly affect complication rates, making the technique appropriate for training programs as well as experienced surgeons.

mcqs.q: In the pedicle tie retrospective, cat reproductive status (intact vs. pregnant vs. in heat), body weight, age, and surgeon experience were all evaluated as potential risk factors. What was the conclusion about these variables?
o: Pregnant cats and cats in heat had significantly higher complication rates and should be referred to specialist surgeons

None of these variables—including surgeon experience level—were significantly associated with pedicle-related complications, supporting the broad applicability of this technique across patient and provider diversity
Body weight was the most important predictor, with obese cats at significantly higher risk of pedicle hemorrhage
Surgeon experience level was the strongest predictor of complications, emphasizing the need for experienced operators in HQHVSN clinics
mcqs.e: None of the tested variables—reproductive status, body weight, age, or surgeon experience—were significantly associated with pedicle complications. This supports using the ovarian pedicle tie technique broadly across HQHVSN settings, including by trainees.

title: Daily gabapentin improved behavior modification progress and decreased stress in shelter cats from hoarding environments in a double-blind randomized placebo-controlled clinical trial
authors: Eagan BH, van Haaften K, Protopopova A
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
citation: Eagan BH, van Haaften K, Protopopova A Daily gabapentin improved behavior modification progress and decreased stress in shelter cats from hoarding environments in a double-blind randomized placebo-controlled clinical trial. Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association. 2023. doi:10.2460/javma.23.01.0044
abstract: Objective: To evaluate the impact of daily gabapentin on behavior modification progression and signs of stress in fearful shelter cats from hoarding environments. Design: Double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial. Animals: 37 cats from hoarding environments (32 met inclusion criteria). Procedures: Healthy fearful cats were entered into either a gabapentin (10 mg/kg PO q12h) or placebo group upon intake. Both groups received daily behavior modification. Daily measures of cat stress score, latency to emerge from hiding, general in-shelter behavior, and urine suppression were collected. Cats were deemed to have graduated from the program when they met behavioral criteria for adoption or upon shelter departure. Results: Of 32 fearful cats, 28 (87.5%) graduated from the behavior modification program in a median of 11 days (range, 4 to 51 days). Animals receiving gabapentin showed greater behavioral improvement over time compared to those given a placebo, including faster progression through the behavior modification program and lower stress scores. Conclusions and Clinical Relevance: Daily gabapentin can improve behavior modification success and reduce stress in fearful shelter cats from hoarding environments. This finding supports the use of gabapentin as an adjunct to behavior modification programs for difficult-to-adopt cats.

mcqs.q: A double-blind RCT tested daily gabapentin in fearful shelter cats from hoarding environments alongside a behavior modification program. What did cats receiving gabapentin show compared to those receiving placebo?
o: No difference in stress scores or program graduation rates
Greater sedation that required dose reduction but improved handling
Greater behavioral improvement over time, faster program completion, and lower stress scores
Improved adoption rates but no difference in in-shelter behavior scores
mcqs.e: Gabapentin-treated cats showed faster progression through behavior modification, lower stress scores, and greater behavioral improvement overall. The RCT design makes this a high-quality evidence base for using gabapentin as an adjunct — not a standalone — tool.

mcqs.q: Nearly 88% of fearful hoarded cats graduated from a behavior modification program in a median of 11 days. What is the clinical relevance of this finding for shelter resource planning?
o: Most hoarded cats require long-term foster care before adoption; 11 days is the minimum observable period only
High graduation rates suggest hoarded fearful cats can be quickly rehabilitated with a structured protocol, supporting intake of this population
The 11-day median means shelters need a minimum 3-week capacity buffer for all hoarded cats
Graduation rates reflect drug effect only; behavior modification without gabapentin is ineffective
mcqs.e: 87.5% graduation in a median 11 days (range 4–51) suggests that most fearful hoarded cats respond well to a structured gabapentin + behavior modification protocol within a timeframe feasible for shelters. This supports intake decisions for this population.

mcqs.q: Based on the gabapentin shelter cat RCT, which statement best describes how gabapentin should be used in shelter behavior programs?
o: As a replacement for behavior modification in fearful cats with severe responses
As an adjunct to — not a substitute for — behavior modification in fearful shelter cats
Only for cats who have failed at least 4 weeks of behavior modification without medication
Exclusively in cats from hoarding environments; evidence does not apply to stray or owner-surrendered fearful cats
mcqs.e: Both groups received behavior modification; gabapentin enhanced outcomes when added. The authors conclude gabapentin 'supports its use as an adjunct to behavior modification programs' — the drug amplifies, not replaces, behavioral work.

title: Vasectomy and ovary-sparing spay in dogs: comparison of health and behavior outcomes with gonadectomized and sexually intact dogs
authors: Zink C, Delgado MM, Stella JL
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
citation: Zink C, Delgado MM, Stella JL Vasectomy and ovary-sparing spay in dogs: comparison of health and behavior outcomes with gonadectomized and sexually intact dogs. Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association. 2023. doi:10.2460/javma.22.08.0382
abstract: Objective: To compare health and behavioral outcomes for dogs that underwent vasectomy or ovary-sparing spay (hysterectomy) with sexually intact dogs or dogs that had undergone traditional castration or ovariohysterectomy. Design: Cross-sectional, web-based survey study. Sample: 6,018 dog owners who responded to a web-based survey between November 3, 2021, and January 7, 2022, providing valid surveys for 6,018 dogs including 1,056 sexually intact, 1,672 castrated, and 58 vasectomized male dogs and 792 sexually intact, 2,281 spayed, and 159 ovary-sparing spayed female dogs. Procedures: Owners were asked questions about orthopedic and other health problems, cancer, and problematic behavior. Results: Longer exposure to gonadal hormones, regardless of reproductive status, was associated with reduced odds of general health problems and both problematic and nuisance behaviors. No significant differences in health outcomes were identified between dogs that had undergone vasectomy versus those that were castrated, or between ovary-sparing spay and traditional spay. However, gonadectomized dogs had higher odds of orthopedic problems compared to sexually intact dogs and those retaining gonads. Conclusions and Clinical Relevance: This study, the first to compare outcomes across all five reproductive statuses, suggests gonadal hormone exposure — regardless of reproductive status — is protective for overall health and behavior. Individualized reproductive surgery decisions should consider the potential health implications of complete gonadectomy.

mcqs.q: Do dogs that undergo vasectomy or ovary-sparing spay (hysterectomy) have different health outcomes compared to traditionally gonadectomized dogs?
o: Yes — vasectomy and ovary-sparing spay produce significantly better orthopedic and overall health outcomes than traditional gonadectomy
No significant differences in health outcomes were found between vasectomy vs. castration or ovary-sparing spay vs. traditional spay
Vasectomy dogs had worse behavioral outcomes due to retained testosterone effects
Ovary-sparing spay dogs had significantly higher cancer rates than traditionally spayed females
mcqs.e: This cross-sectional survey of 6,018 dogs found no significant differences in health outcomes between dogs with vasectomy vs. castration or between ovary-sparing spay vs. traditional spay. However, a key finding was that gonadectomized dogs (all types) had higher odds of orthopedic problems compared to sexually intact dogs and those retaining gonads. This supports the concept that gonadal hormone exposure — regardless of reproductive status — is protective for musculoskeletal health.

mcqs.q: A dog owner is considering vasectomy instead of castration to preserve hormonal benefits. What does the best available evidence show about reproductive-status-retaining procedures versus traditional gonadectomy?
o: Vasectomy clearly outperforms castration for orthopedic and behavioral outcomes, making it the preferred choice for all male dogs

Gonadal hormone retention (whether via intact status, vasectomy, or ovary-sparing spay) is associated with reduced odds of orthopedic problems, but no health differences were found between vasectomy and castration specifically
Vasectomy is only beneficial for large breeds prone to CCL rupture; small dogs show no difference
Castrated dogs have better behavioral outcomes than vasectomized dogs due to lower testosterone-driven aggression
mcqs.e: The study found that longer gonadal hormone exposure was associated with reduced odds of orthopedic problems and problematic behaviors, regardless of reproductive status. However, when comparing vasectomy to castration directly, no significant health outcome differences were identified. The same applied to ovary-sparing spay vs. traditional spay. The protective effect appears to come from retaining the gonads, not the reproductive organs — a distinction that supports individualized discussions about surgical options.

title: Natural history of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in cats from rehoming centers: The CatScan II study
authors: Novo Matos J, Payne JR, Seo J, Luis Fuentes V
journal: Journal of Veterinary Internal Medicine
citation: Novo Matos J, Payne JR, Seo J, Luis Fuentes V Natural history of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in cats from rehoming centers: The CatScan II study. Journal of Veterinary Internal Medicine. 2022. doi:10.1111/jvim.16576
abstract: Background: The natural history of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) in cats has been mainly studied in cats referred for suspected heart disease. Few data are available on factors associated with development of HCM in cats without clinical signs at baseline. Objectives: To characterize the natural history of HCM in cats from rehoming centers and identify echocardiographic variables associated with HCM development. Animals: One hundred seven cats from UK rehoming centers without a history of clinical signs of cardiac or systemic disease at the time of adoption. Methods: Prospective longitudinal study. After rehoming, cats were reexamined with serial echocardiography over a median follow-up of 5.6 years. Results: At baseline, 68 cats were echocardiographically normal, 18 were equivocal, and 21 had HCM. Nineteen additional cats developed HCM during follow-up. Lower left atrial fractional shortening, higher left ventricular fractional shortening, and higher body weight at baseline predicted HCM development. Cardiovascular events occurred in 21% of cats with HCM. Conclusions and Clinical Relevance: Lower left atrial systolic function appears to precede overt HCM in cats from rehoming centers. The prevalence of HCM in this unselected population was substantial, and cardiovascular events occurred in a meaningful proportion of affected cats, highlighting the importance of cardiac screening in shelter and rehoming populations.

mcqs.q: In a prospective study of 107 cats adopted from UK rehoming centres, what was found about the burden of HCM over a median follow-up of 5.6 years?
o: HCM was rare in this unselected population, affecting fewer than 5% of cats
HCM prevalence was substantial (~37% of cats were affected), and cardiovascular events occurred in 21% of those with HCM
All cats that were echocardiographically normal at baseline remained free of HCM throughout follow-up
HCM was detected only in cats already showing clinical signs at the time of adoption
mcqs.e: At baseline 21 cats had HCM; 19 additional cats developed HCM during follow-up, giving a total of 40/107 (~37%) affected — a substantial prevalence in this unselected rehoming population. Cardiovascular events (a separate statistic) occurred in 21% of the HCM-positive cats. Both findings highlight the importance of cardiac screening at adoption.

mcqs.q: Certain baseline echocardiographic variables predicted which cats would go on to develop HCM. What is the clinical significance of identifying lower left atrial fractional shortening before overt HCM develops?
o: It confirms that HCM is always preceded by obvious clinical signs detectable at adoption
Left atrial dysfunction may be a preclinical marker, suggesting cardiac screening at adoption can identify cats at elevated risk before disease becomes overt
Left atrial shortening fraction has no predictive value and routine cardiac screening is not warranted
This finding only applies to pedigree cats and does not inform screening of shelter populations
mcqs.e: Lower left atrial fractional shortening appeared to precede overt HCM, suggesting it is a preclinical marker. Combined with the substantial overall HCM prevalence in this unselected population, the study supports the importance of cardiac screening in rehoming centre cats.

title: Renal amyloid-A amyloidosis in cats: Characterization of proteinuria and biomarker discovery, and associations with kidney histology
authors: Palizzotto C, Ferri F, Callegari C, Rossi F, Manfredi M, Carcangiu L, Gerardi G, Ferro S, Cavicchioli L, Müller E, Weiss M, Vogt AC, Lavatelli F, Ricagno S, Hurley K, Zini E
journal: Journal of Veterinary Internal Medicine
citation: Palizzotto C, Ferri F, Callegari C, Rossi F, Manfredi M, Carcangiu L, Gerardi G, Ferro S, Cavicchioli L, Müller E, Weiss M, Vogt AC, Lavatelli F, Ricagno S, Hurley K, Zini E Renal amyloid-A amyloidosis in cats: Characterization of proteinuria and biomarker discovery, and associations with kidney histology. Journal of Veterinary Internal Medicine. 2024. doi:10.1111/jvim.16920
abstract: Background: Systemic AA amyloidosis recently was shown to have a high prevalence in shelter cats in Italy and was associated with azotemia and proteinuria. Objectives: To investigate urine protein profiles and identify diagnostic biomarkers in cats with renal AA amyloidosis. Animals: Twenty-nine shelter cats. Methods: Case-control study. Cats with renal proteinuria that died or were euthanized between 2018 and 2021 were included. Histology was used to characterize renal damage; immunohistochemistry confirmed AA amyloidosis. Urine protein-to-creatinine (UPC) and urine amyloid A-to-creatinine (UAAC) ratios were calculated. Urine protein profiling was done using sodium dodecyl sulfate-agarose gel electrophoresis (SDS-AGE) and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Results: Nineteen cats had AA amyloidosis. Affected cats had higher UPC and UAAC ratios than unaffected cats. Mixed proteinuria was identified in 89.4% of affected cats. LC-MS identified 63 potential biomarkers; urine apolipoprotein C-III was higher in cats with AA amyloidosis. AA amyloidosis was associated with glomerulosclerosis and interstitial fibrosis. Conclusions and Clinical Relevance: Renal AA amyloidosis in shelter cats is associated with mixed proteinuria, specific kidney lesions, and elevated urine biomarkers. Urine apolipoprotein C-III may assist in diagnosis. Further research is needed regarding the role of lipid transport proteins in this condition.

mcqs.q: What urine abnormality pattern should prompt consideration of renal AA amyloidosis in shelter cats?
o: Isolated hematuria with no proteinuria
Mixed proteinuria (both glomerular and tubular patterns) with elevated UPC ratio
Dilute urine (isosthenuria) without proteinuria
Pyuria with glucosuria suggesting tubular dysfunction
mcqs.e: In this case-control study of 29 shelter cats, those with renal AA amyloidosis had higher UPC and urine amyloid A-to-creatinine ratios than unaffected cats. Mixed proteinuria (both glomerular and tubular) was found in 89.4% of affected cats. Urine apolipoprotein C-III was also elevated and identified as a potential diagnostic biomarker. AA amyloidosis should be considered in the differential for shelter cats with proteinuria and CKD.

mcqs.q: What histologic lesions are characteristically associated with renal AA amyloidosis in shelter cats, based on this case-control study?
o: Lymphoplasmacytic interstitial nephritis without glomerular involvement
Glomerulosclerosis and interstitial fibrosis, confirmed alongside amyloid deposits by immunohistochemistry
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis as the predominant lesion without tubular involvement
Subcapsular cortical infarcts with renal arteritis
mcqs.e: In this case-control study of 29 shelter cats (19 with AA amyloidosis), renal AA amyloidosis was associated with glomerulosclerosis and interstitial fibrosis. Amyloid was confirmed by immunohistochemistry and mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Affected cats also had higher UPC and urine amyloid A-to-creatinine ratios, and mixed proteinuria was present in 89.4% of affected cats. Recognizing this histologic pattern supports identification of a distinct CKD pathway in shelter cat populations.

title: Feline panleukopenia virus DNA shedding following modified live virus vaccination in a shelter setting
authors: Jacobson LS, Janke KJ, Ha K, Giacinti JA, Weese JS
journal: The Veterinary Journal
citation: Jacobson LS, Janke KJ, Ha K, Giacinti JA, Weese JS Feline panleukopenia virus DNA shedding following modified live virus vaccination in a shelter setting. The Veterinary Journal. 2022. doi:10.1016/j.tvjl.2021.105783
abstract: This study assessed the frequency and timing of feline panleukopenia virus (FPV) DNA shedding in feces following administration of a modified live FPV vaccine in a shelter setting. Feces were collected from 37 shelter cats that did not meet clinical criteria for panleukopenia on the day of vaccination (day 0) or on days 3, 7, 14, and 21 post-vaccination. A commercial quantitative PCR (qPCR) fecal pathogen panel and a canine parvovirus point-of-care antigen test were performed on each sample. Positive qPCR results were obtained from 8/37 cats (21.6%) without clinical signs, primarily on day 7. DNA copy numbers were substantially lower following vaccination than in clinically infected cats. The point-of-care antigen test was negative in all vaccinated cats. FPV qPCR cannot differentiate subclinical infection from vaccine virus shedding. The authors recommend limiting PCR testing to cats with strong clinical suspicion of panleukopenia and considering recent vaccination timing when interpreting results, to avoid unnecessary outbreak responses based on false-positive PCR results in vaccinated shelter cats.

mcqs.q: A shelter study found that 21.6% of vaccinated clinically well cats shed FPV DNA by qPCR, primarily on day 7 post-vaccination. What is the key clinical implication?
o: Modified live FPV vaccine should not be used in shelter settings due to unacceptable shedding rates
A positive fecal qPCR result in a recently vaccinated asymptomatic shelter cat should not automatically trigger an outbreak response
Vaccinated cats shedding FPV DNA should be isolated for 21 days to prevent spread to other cats
qPCR is unreliable in vaccinated cats and should be replaced by SNAP testing for post-vaccination surveillance
mcqs.e: 21.6% of vaccinated clinically well cats had positive qPCR results, primarily at day 7, but the point-of-care antigen test was negative in all vaccinated cats. qPCR cannot distinguish vaccine shedding from subclinical natural infection — so a positive qPCR in a recently vaccinated, clinically well cat should not trigger unnecessary isolation or outbreak procedures.

mcqs.q: When is fecal qPCR testing most appropriately used to diagnose feline panleukopenia in a shelter setting?
o: Routinely in all cats at intake, because positive results always indicate natural infection
In cats with strong clinical suspicion of panleukopenia, with recent vaccination timing considered in interpretation
At day 7 post-vaccination as a routine quality check to confirm immune response
Only after two consecutive negative SNAP tests to confirm clinical resolution before adoption
mcqs.e: The authors recommend limiting FPV PCR testing to cats with strong clinical suspicion of panleukopenia and emphasize considering vaccination timing when interpreting results. Post-vaccination shedding at day 7 can produce qPCR positives in well cats, making indiscriminate testing counterproductive and potentially triggering unnecessary outbreak responses.

title: Identification of spayed and neutered cats and dogs: Veterinary training and compliance with practice guidelines
authors: Mielo MR, Amirian ES, Levy JK
journal: The Veterinary Journal
citation: Mielo MR, Amirian ES, Levy JK Identification of spayed and neutered cats and dogs: Veterinary training and compliance with practice guidelines. The Veterinary Journal. 2022. doi:10.1016/j.tvjl.2022.105856
abstract: Spay/neuter identification tattoos and ear-tipping are simple, cost-effective methods to minimize unnecessary anesthesia and surgery in companion animals, or the misidentification of sexually intact animals. This study assessed training of sterilization identifiers in US and Canadian veterinary schools and practitioner compliance with guidelines for identifiers via surveys conducted in 2019. Faculty in all 34 participating veterinary schools reported curricula included sterilization identifiers in 31% of lecture-based training, 75% of spay/neuter laboratory-based training, and 38% of clinical practice-based training. A total of 425 facilities performing spay/neuter reported frequency and technical aspects of sterilization identifiers. Facilities encountering large numbers of animals of unknown background, performing a high number of surgeries, or with specialized spay/neuter training were significantly more likely to use identifiers. Only 5% of private practices tattooed all owned animals and 21% tattooed all unowned animals. In contrast, 80% of shelters and 72% of spay/neuter clinics tattooed animals. Green tattoos placed near surgical incisions represented the predominant technique. Enhanced training and broader implementation of sterilization identification best practices are essential to prevent unnecessary surgeries and unintended breeding in animals misidentified as sexually intact.

mcqs.q: A feral cat arrives at a shelter with no history. You perform an exploratory laparotomy assuming she is intact, but find no reproductive organs. Which practice, if it had been followed consistently, would most have prevented this unnecessary surgery?
o: Routine pre-surgical bloodwork to confirm intact status
Use of sterilization identification—specifically a green tattoo placed near the surgical incision at time of original surgery
Mandatory microchip lookup before all surgeries
Pre-surgical vaginal cytology to assess estrogen influence
mcqs.e: The study confirmed that green tattoos placed near the surgical incision are the predominant and recommended sterilization identification technique. Only 80% of shelters and 72% of spay/neuter clinics routinely tattooed animals; just 5% of private practices tattooed all owned animals. Broader use of tattoos would prevent unnecessary surgeries in animals of unknown background.

mcqs.q: A veterinary school is revising its curriculum on sterilization identification. Survey data show that while laboratory training covers the topic in 75% of schools, lecture-based training covers it in only 31%. What does the study's finding about adoption of identifiers by facility type suggest about how training translates to practice?
o: Training format does not matter—adoption of identifiers is driven mainly by the volume of surgeries performed

Facilities with specialized spay/neuter training, high surgical volume, or animals of unknown background are significantly more likely to use identifiers, suggesting that hands-on training and contextual experience drive adoption
Private practices are equally likely to use identifiers as shelters when given the same training
Lecture-based training is the most effective format because it reaches the most students
mcqs.e: The study found that facilities encountering large numbers of animals of unknown background, performing high surgery volumes, or with specialized spay/neuter training were significantly more likely to use identifiers. This pattern suggests that experiential, context-relevant training—not just lecture exposure—and the practical need created by treating animals of unknown history drive identifier adoption.

title: Capturing free-roaming dogs for sterilisation: A multi-site study in Goa, India
authors: Fielding HR, Fernandes KA, Amulya VR, Belgayer D, Misquita A, Kenny R, Gibson AD, Gamble L, Bronsvoort BMdC, Mellanby RJ, Mazeri S
journal: Preventive Veterinary Medicine
citation: Fielding HR, Fernandes KA, Amulya VR, Belgayer D, Misquita A, Kenny R, Gibson AD, Gamble L, Bronsvoort BMdC, Mellanby RJ, Mazeri S Capturing free-roaming dogs for sterilisation: A multi-site study in Goa, India. Preventive Veterinary Medicine. 2023. doi:10.1016/j.prevetmed.2023.105996
abstract: Street and free-roaming dog populations in lowand middle-income countries pose public health risks including rabies transmission. Surgical sterilisation campaigns are a key component of humane dog population management. This multi-site study documented dog capture rates across six sterilization campaigns in Goa, India, using spatial coordinates and population surveys to assess campaign efficiency. Results demonstrate that as sterilization coverage increases within a community, capturing remaining intact dogs becomes progressively more difficult, with corresponding escalation in unit costs per dog captured. The study quantified diminishing returns on capture efficiency as the proportion of sterilized animals rises. These findings have important implications for planning efficient, cost-effective dog population management interventions: targeting areas of lower coverage first and adapting capture strategies as coverage improves may maximize program impact. Understanding capture dynamics is essential for sustainable free-roaming dog population control programs.

mcqs.q: A multi-site study in Goa, India found that as sterilization coverage increased in an area, capturing remaining intact dogs became progressively harder and more expensive. What is the key planning implication for dog population management programs?
o: Programs should maintain a constant capture effort throughout, as coverage level does not affect capture efficiency

Program planners should anticipate diminishing returns: capture efficiency decreases as coverage rises, so unit costs will escalate in later program phases, requiring adaptive strategies (e.g., different trapping methods, higher effort) to reach the last intact animals
The most cost-effective strategy is to achieve 50% coverage and then stop, as diminishing returns make further efforts uneconomical
High-coverage areas should switch to lethal control because capture of remaining intact dogs is too expensive
mcqs.e: The study quantified progressive capture difficulty as coverage increased. Planners must budget for escalating unit costs in later phases and develop adaptive strategies for reaching the remaining intact population—the herd that is hardest to capture but most important to sterilize for population-level impact.

mcqs.q: The Goa dog sterilization study used spatial coordinates and population surveys to document capture dynamics. What does this methodological approach add to program planning that simple sterilization counts cannot?
o: Spatial data are unnecessary for dog population management programs; total sterilization counts are sufficient to guide decisions

Spatial and population survey data reveal where coverage gaps exist and how capture efficiency varies across sites, enabling targeted allocation of trapping effort to areas with the lowest coverage and highest intact dog density
Population surveys are only useful at program initiation; they add no value once sterilization campaigns are underway
Spatial coordinates are needed only to comply with research ethics requirements and have no operational value
mcqs.e: Spatial mapping revealed site-level variation in coverage and capture success. This allows programs to target trapping resources where intact dog density is highest and coverage is lowest—a more efficient strategy than uniformly applying effort across all areas.

title: Frequency of SARS-CoV-2 infection in dogs and cats: Results of a retrospective serological survey in Šumadija District, Serbia
authors: Stanojevic S, Radojicic S, Misic D, Srejic D, Vasiljevic DV, Prokic K, Ilic N
journal: Preventive Veterinary Medicine
citation: Stanojevic S, Radojicic S, Misic D, Srejic D, Vasiljevic DV, Prokic K, Ilic N Frequency of SARS-CoV-2 infection in dogs and cats: Results of a retrospective serological survey in Šumadija District, Serbia. Preventive Veterinary Medicine. 2022. doi:10.1016/j.prevetmed.2022.105755
abstract: This retrospective serosurvey examined SARS-CoV-2 exposure in companion and stray animals in Šumadija District, Serbia, during the COVID-19 pandemic. A total of samples from dogs and cats were tested using a neutralization assay. The relative frequency of SARS-CoV-2 infection in dogs was 1.45% and in cats was 5.56%. Pet owner seropositivity was 11%, and seropositivity in pets with close owner contact was 9%. Stray animals showed lower seroprevalence compared to household pets. The results confirm that companion dogs and cats are susceptible to SARS-CoV-2, with cats showing higher seroprevalence than dogs. Human-to-pet transmission was identified as the primary infection route. Findings emphasize the importance of One Health surveillance including companion and stray animals during respiratory virus pandemics.

mcqs.q: In a retrospective SARS-CoV-2 serosurvey of companion and stray animals, which species showed higher seroprevalence, and which group had higher exposure than stray animals?
o: Dogs had higher seroprevalence than cats; stray animals had higher seroprevalence than household pets
Cats had higher seroprevalence than dogs; household pets with close owner contact showed higher seropositivity than strays
Dogs and cats had equal seroprevalence; stray animals had higher exposure due to less controlled environments
Cats had higher seroprevalence and stray cats showed higher exposure than household cats
