mcqs.e: Cats (5.56%) showed higher SARS-CoV-2 seroprevalence than dogs (1.45%). Household pets with close owner contact had 9% seropositivity versus lower rates in stray animals, confirming human-to-pet transmission as the primary infection route.

mcqs.q: What does the higher SARS-CoV-2 seroprevalence in cats compared to dogs suggest for shelter and veterinary practice?
o: Cats pose a greater zoonotic risk than dogs and should be tested before any clinical contact
Cats are more susceptible to SARS-CoV-2 from human sources and warrant inclusion in One Health surveillance frameworks
Dogs are effectively resistant to SARS-CoV-2 and need no monitoring in shelter or pandemic settings
The difference is not clinically meaningful because both species have overall low seroprevalence
mcqs.e: Cats had consistently higher SARS-CoV-2 seroprevalence than dogs across multiple studies. This greater susceptibility — combined with human-to-pet transmission being the primary route — supports including cats in One Health surveillance and highlights them as a more sensitive indicator species for household COVID-19 exposure.

title: Top-down animal welfare crisis communication during the COVID-19 pandemic: Animal care worker information sources, self-perceived knowledge and welfare concerns
authors: Miller SL, Kwan JX, Dalton KR, Waite KB, Davis MF
journal: The Veterinary Record
citation: Miller SL, Kwan JX, Dalton KR, Waite KB, Davis MF Top-down animal welfare crisis communication during the COVID-19 pandemic: Animal care worker information sources, self-perceived knowledge and welfare concerns. The Veterinary Record. 2025. doi:10.1002/vetr.5498
abstract: This cross-sectional study assessed animal care worker responses to identify factors valuable for crisis preparedness planning during the COVID-19 pandemic. Participants included small animal veterinary workers (n = 1,209) and shelter/rescue workers (n = 132). Shelter and rescue workers (SRC workers) more often reported frequent communication from their organization, self-perceived expert knowledge, and having welfare concerns related to the pandemic compared to veterinary workers. Information sources differed significantly by worker type, with SRC workers relying more heavily on organizational communications. The study highlights a potential need for increased, more harmonized crisis communication from leading public and animal health entities to better support both veterinary and shelter worker populations. Differences in crisis communication patterns between private practice and shelter workers may affect their ability to implement appropriate biosecurity and animal welfare measures during future public health emergencies.

mcqs.q: During the COVID-19 pandemic, shelter/rescue workers and veterinary workers differed in their information sources and communication experiences. What pattern was found?
o: Veterinary workers reported more frequent organizational communication and higher self-perceived knowledge than shelter workers

Shelter/rescue workers more often reported frequent organizational communication and higher self-perceived knowledge, but relied more on their own organizations rather than broader public health entities
Both worker types reported equal reliance on government public health sources for COVID-19 guidance
Shelter workers had lower welfare concerns than veterinary workers because their patients could not contract COVID-19
mcqs.e: Shelter and rescue workers more often reported frequent organizational communication, self-perceived expert knowledge, and welfare concerns compared to veterinary workers — but they relied more heavily on organizational communications rather than broader public/animal health authorities. This divergence in information sourcing may affect crisis response consistency.

mcqs.q: What is the key preparedness implication from the COVID-19 crisis communication study for animal care organizations?
o: Shelter workers require less external guidance because they have strong internal communication channels
Leading public and animal health entities should provide more harmonized, proactive crisis communication to support both shelter and veterinary worker populations
Crisis communication should be exclusively channeled through professional veterinary associations rather than government bodies
Social media should be recognized as the primary reliable information source for shelter workers during crises
mcqs.e: Differences in information sourcing between shelter and veterinary workers — with shelter workers relying more on internal communications — highlight a potential gap in standardized guidance during crises. The study calls for more harmonized, proactive communication from leading public and animal health authorities to reduce this disparity.

title: How do accessible veterinary care providers evaluate programmes and engage communities? Results of a qualitative analysis of Canadian service providers
authors: Rausch Q, Geddes N, Liao TP, Van Patter L
journal: The Veterinary Record
citation: Rausch Q, Geddes N, Liao TP, Van Patter L How do accessible veterinary care providers evaluate programmes and engage communities? Results of a qualitative analysis of Canadian service providers. The Veterinary Record. 2026. doi:10.1002/vetr.6022
abstract: Accessible veterinary care (AVC) programmes aim to reduce barriers to veterinary services for under-resourced pet owners and communities. This qualitative study examined 18 Canadian accessible veterinary care providers through focus groups and interviews to understand how they evaluate their programmes and engage with communities. Analysis revealed large diversity in programme initiation, evolution, and evaluation approaches. Concerns identified included ethical challenges around community engagement, funder reporting requirements creating administrative burden, and limited knowledge and resources for rigorous programme evaluation. Providers highlighted the need for standardized metrics and evaluation frameworks to demonstrate programme impact. The study underscores the importance of community-centred, culturally appropriate service delivery and the need for better infrastructure to support AVC provider capacity for evaluation and long-term programme sustainability.

mcqs.q: A qualitative study of 18 Canadian accessible veterinary care (AVC) providers identified gaps in how programmes are evaluated. What was the central finding?
o: Most AVC providers use rigorous standardised outcome metrics and need no additional support
There is wide diversity in programme evaluation approaches, with limited capacity for rigorous evaluation and a need for standardised metrics
Funders were found to be the primary obstacle to programme evaluation
AVC providers consistently prioritised community engagement over measurable health outcomes
mcqs.e: The study found large diversity in evaluation approaches, limited knowledge and resources for rigorous evaluation, and a clear need for standardised metrics and evaluation frameworks — providers recognised this gap themselves as a constraint on demonstrating programme impact.

mcqs.q: What ethical challenges did accessible veterinary care providers in this study identify regarding community engagement?
o: Providing free services was seen as creating dependency and undermining community agency
Providers reported no ethical concerns — community engagement was uniformly positive
Challenges included ensuring culturally appropriate, community-centred service delivery and managing funder reporting requirements that created administrative burden
Ethical concerns were limited to professional scope-of-practice questions
mcqs.e: Ethical challenges identified included the need for culturally appropriate and community-centred approaches, funder reporting requirements that created administrative burden, and limited resources for proper evaluation — all of which affect programme sustainability and integrity.

title: Shelter dogs as reservoirs of international clones of Escherichia coli carrying mcr-1.1 and bla(CTX-M) resistance genes in Lima, Peru
authors: Ayzanoa B, Salvatierra G, Cuicapuza D, Furlan JPR, Sellera FP, Chavez L, Esposito F, Tsukayama P, Lincopan N
journal: Veterinary Microbiology
citation: Ayzanoa B, Salvatierra G, Cuicapuza D, Furlan JPR, Sellera FP, Chavez L, Esposito F, Tsukayama P, Lincopan N Shelter dogs as reservoirs of international clones of Escherichia coli carrying mcr-1.1 and bla(CTX-M) resistance genes in Lima, Peru. Veterinary Microbiology. 2025. doi:10.1016/j.vetmic.2025.110543
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical public health threat worldwide, particularly at the human-animal interface where cross-transmission of critical priority Enterobacterales, such as Escherichia coli, have become increasingly reported. Worryingly, E. coli encoding extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs) has been documented in companion animals worldwide. Conversely, the presence of mcr genes, which confer resistance to polymyxins, in bacteria from pets remains more infrequent. In this study, we sequenced and reported on the first genomic data of E. coli strains carrying mcr-1 and/or blaCTX-M genes isolated from rectal swabs of stray dogs in a shelter in the city of Lima, Peru. Antimicrobial susceptibility revealed that E. coli strains exhibited a multidrug resistance profile. In addition to mcr-1 and blaCTX-M genes, other clinically relevant resistance determinants were identified, with notably presence of blaTEM-176 and the novel blaSCO-2 variant. The association of mcr-1.1 and IncI2 plasmid was confirmed. Several virulence genes were detected, classifying strains as putative extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli. Multilocus sequence typing prediction recognized diverse sequence types (ST), including ST155, ST189, ST657, ST746, ST1140, ST3014, and ST7188. This study represents the first report of mcr-positive E. coli in dogs from Peru, emphasizing the need for continuous surveillance and genomic characterization to better understand the transmission dynamics of these critical resistance genes at the human-animal interface. Furthermore, our results provide evidence that stray, and shelter dogs could be a reservoir for the spread of WHO priority pathogens, and/or polymyxin and β-lactam resistance genes, which is a public health and One Health concern that requires appropriate management strategies.

mcqs.q: The detection of mcr-1 and blaCTX-M genes in shelter dogs in Peru is most significant because:
o: It confirms that shelter dogs cause most E. coli infections in people in South America
It demonstrates that shelter dogs can harbor WHO-priority antimicrobial resistance genes on mobile genetic elements linked to international high-risk clone lineages
It proves that colistin use in companion animals should be banned globally
It shows that blaCTX-M infections in dogs are untreatable with any currently available antibiotic
mcqs.e: mcr-1 confers resistance to colistin (a last-resort antibiotic) and is plasmid-mediated (mobile), while blaCTX-M confers extended-spectrum beta-lactamase activity. Their presence in shelter dogs matching international high-risk clones establishes shelters as nodes in a global AMR transmission network — a One Health priority.

mcqs.q: From a One Health shelter management perspective, the finding of plasmid-mediated colistin resistance (mcr-1) in Lima shelter dogs implies:
o: Colistin should be used to treat all shelter dogs as a prophylactic measure
Shelter dogs pose no AMR risk as long as they are not in contact with immunocompromised humans
AMR surveillance programs in shelters are warranted globally, as shelter dog populations may serve as reservoirs for resistance genes of human medical importance
The finding is limited to Peru and has no implications for shelters in other countries
mcqs.e: The strains matched international clone lineages, demonstrating cross-border AMR transmission pathways. This supports implementing AMR surveillance in shelter populations globally — not just in resource-limited settings — as part of a One Health approach.

title: Streptococcus zooepidemicus in dogs: Exploring a canine pathogen through multilocus sequence typing
authors: Mangano ER, Jones GMC, Suarez-Bonnet A, Waller AS, Priestnall SL
journal: Veterinary Microbiology
citation: Mangano ER, Jones GMC, Suarez-Bonnet A, Waller AS, Priestnall SL Streptococcus zooepidemicus in dogs: Exploring a canine pathogen through multilocus sequence typing. Veterinary Microbiology. 2024. doi:10.1016/j.vetmic.2024.110059
abstract: Streptococcus equi. subsp. zooepidemicus (S. zooepidemicus) associated diseases in dogs have emerged as a significant concern over recent decades. S. zooepidemicus occurs sporadically in dog populations globally, with increased prevalence in shelters/kennels. This study used multilocus sequence typing (MLST) of 149 independent canine S. zooepidemicus isolates to assess associations between sequence type and breed, country of origin, disease severity, sampling type, year, and behaviour within an outbreak. No clear associations for breed, country, sampling type and year were determined in this study. ST-10 and 123 strains were present within all disease categories, from no clinical signs to severe disease. Assessment of S. zooepidemicus infection in 3 UK outbreaks at the same location found ST-10, 18, 123 strains, and a ST-173 strain in a US outbreak, were associated with haemorrhagic pneumonia and persisted in kennelled populations over time. The ST-173 clonal complex has been noted to have severe virulence capabilities in dogs and other species. S. zooepidemicus seems to thrive in environments with a high risk of transmissibility, overcrowding, stress and naïve populations, particularly for those in shelters/kennels. MLST alone cannot determine the virulence phenotype of S. zooepidemicus in dogs. However, a level of conservancy and diversity within ST allelic loci aids the opportunity to cause severe disease in dogs. Thus, further research into whole genome sequencing and characterising the virulence factors of S. zooepidemicus is warranted in dogs.

mcqs.q: Regarding Streptococcus zooepidemicus virulence in dogs, what did multilocus sequence typing (MLST) of 149 canine isolates reveal about the relationship between sequence type and disease severity?
o: Specific sequence types reliably predicted disease severity, allowing MLST to guide clinical management
ST-10 and ST-123 strains were present across all disease categories from asymptomatic to severe, meaning MLST alone cannot predict virulence phenotype
Only the ST-173 clonal complex was associated with severe disease; other sequence types caused only mild illness
MLST showed that country of origin was the strongest predictor of disease severity in S. zoo infections
mcqs.e: ST-10 and ST-123 strains were found across the full spectrum of disease severity — from no clinical signs to haemorrhagic pneumonia. MLST alone cannot determine virulence phenotype. While ST-173 has noted virulence capabilities, sequence typing alone is insufficient for clinical risk prediction, and whole genome sequencing is recommended for further characterization.

mcqs.q: In shelter settings, which conditions are most likely to promote S. zooepidemicus emergence and spread in dogs?
o: Cold temperatures and dry environments, which favor bacterial survival on surfaces
Overcrowding, stress, high transmissibility environments, and naive populations — typical conditions in shelters and kennels
Frequent antibiotic exposure, which selects for resistant S. zoo strains
Contact with poultry and waterfowl, which are the primary reservoir for canine S. zoo
mcqs.e: S. zooepidemicus thrives in environments with high transmissibility risk, overcrowding, stress, and immunologically naive populations — precisely the conditions common in shelters and kennels. Understanding these risk factors supports targeted surveillance and preventive interventions in these settings.

title: Canine parvovirus is shed infrequently by cats without diarrhoea in multi-cat environments
authors: Carrai M, Decaro N, Van Brussel K, Dall'Ara P, Desario C, Fracasso M, Šlapeta J, Colombo E, Bo S, Beatty JA, Meers J, Barrs VR
journal: Veterinary Microbiology
citation: Carrai M, Decaro N, Van Brussel K, Dall'Ara P, Desario C, Fracasso M, Šlapeta J, Colombo E, Bo S, Beatty JA, Meers J, Barrs VR Canine parvovirus is shed infrequently by cats without diarrhoea in multi-cat environments. Veterinary Microbiology. 2021. doi:10.1016/j.vetmic.2021.109204
abstract: Whether subclinical shedding of canine parvovirus (CPV) by cats might contribute to the epidemiology of canine CPV infections, particularly in facilities housing both cats and dogs, requires clarification. Conflicting results are reported to date. Using conventional PCR (cPCR) to amplify the VP2 gene, shedding of the CPV variants (CPV-2a, 2b, 2c) by healthy cats in multi-cat environments was reportedly common in Europe but rare in Australia. The aim of this study was to determine whether low-level faecal CPV shedding occurs in multi-cat environments in Australia and Italy using a TaqMan real-time PCR to detect Carnivore protoparvovirus 1 (CPV and feline parvovirus, FPV) DNA, and minor-groove binder probe real-time PCR assay to differentiate FPV and CPV types and to characterize CPV variants. In total, 741 non-diarrhoeic faecal samples from shelters in Australia (n = 263) and from shelters or cat colonies in Italy (n = 478) were tested. Overall, Carnivore protoparvovirus 1 DNA was detected in 49 of 741 (6.61%) samples. Differentiation was possible for 31 positive samples. FPV was most common among positive samples (28/31, 90.3%). CPV was detected in 4/31 samples (12.9%) including CPV-2a in one sample, CPV-2b in another and co-infections of FPV/CPV-2b and CPV-2a/CPV-2b in the remaining two samples. A high rate of subclinical FPV infection was detected in one shelter during an outbreak of feline panleukopenia, during which 21 of 22 asymptomatic cats (95.5%) sampled were shedding FPV. Faecal shedding of CPV by cats in multi-cat environments is uncommon suggesting that domestic cats are not significant reservoirs of CPV.

mcqs.q: Should cats housed alongside dogs in mixed-species shelters be considered a significant reservoir for canine parvovirus (CPV) transmission to dogs?
o: Yes — studies show cats frequently shed CPV and are a primary transmission source in mixed-species facilities
No — CPV shedding by non-diarrhoeic cats is uncommon, and domestic cats are not considered significant CPV reservoirs
Yes — but only in shelters in Europe where CPV-2c variant prevalence is higher than in Australia
The evidence is too conflicting to make any recommendation about cats as CPV reservoirs
mcqs.e: Using sensitive real-time PCR on 741 non-diarrhoeic fecal samples from shelters in Australia and Italy, CPV was detected in only 4/31 typeable positive samples (12.9%), with FPV accounting for 90.3%. The study concludes that faecal CPV shedding by cats is uncommon and domestic cats are not significant CPV reservoirs.

mcqs.q: During a feline panleukopenia outbreak, a shelter found that 95.5% of asymptomatic cats were shedding FPV by qPCR. What does this mean for infection control decision-making?
o: Asymptomatic cats shedding FPV need not be isolated because shedding without clinical signs is never infectious
High rates of subclinical FPV shedding during outbreaks mean that clinical signs alone dramatically underestimate the true scope of infection and exposure
Subclinical FPV shedding only occurs in vaccinated cats, so the outbreak population was likely previously immune
qPCR positivity in asymptomatic cats reflects environmental contamination on fur rather than active shedding
mcqs.e: During a panleukopenia outbreak, 21/22 asymptomatic cats (95.5%) were shedding FPV. This demonstrates that clinical signs capture only a fraction of the infected population during outbreaks. Relying solely on clinical presentation to identify isolation candidates will severely underestimate exposure risk and transmission potential.

title: Isolation and characterization of Chlamydia felis and its pathogenesis in cats
authors: Chen J, Long J, Zhou H, Huang C, Zhu Y, Wang R, Zhang H, Qin Y, Ouyang K, Wei Z, Huang W, Chen Y
journal: Veterinary Microbiology
citation: Chen J, Long J, Zhou H, Huang C, Zhu Y, Wang R, Zhang H, Qin Y, Ouyang K, Wei Z, Huang W, Chen Y Isolation and characterization of Chlamydia felis and its pathogenesis in cats. Veterinary Microbiology. 2024. doi:10.1016/j.vetmic.2024.110128
abstract: Feline upper respiratory tract disease (URTD) is a common but complicated disease that occurs in domestic cats, worldwide. 396 cats in Guangxi Province, China were screened for URTD-associated pathogens from March 2022 to August 2023. Mycoplasma felis was found to be the most prevalent infectious agent with a positivity rate of 24.75%, followed by feline calicivirus (FCV), Chlamydia felis, feline herpesvirus 1 (FHV-1) and feline influenza A virus (FeIAV) with rates of 15.91, 11.62, 5.56 and 1.52%, respectively. In particular, C. felis and M. felis were found in 13 of 55 co-infected cats. Of the 46 C. felis-positive samples, one strain, named as GXNN36, was successfully isolated using chicken embryos and it was characterized both in vivo and in vitro. For the cat studies, both highand low-dose challenged groups showed severe conjunctivitis, accompanied by transient fever and respiratory symptoms. C. felis replicated well in turbinate, trachea and lung tissues with high copy numbers and the infection subsequently spread to the livers, spleens, pancreas, kidneys, hearts and intestines. These findings will help our understanding of the role of C. felis in feline URTD and provide a valuable model to evaluate the efficacy of vaccines and therapeutic remedies in the future.

mcqs.q: In a Chinese screening study of cats with upper respiratory tract disease (URTD), which pathogen was most prevalent, and what was the significance of Chlamydia felis co-infection?
o: Feline herpesvirus-1 was most prevalent; Chlamydia felis rarely occurred as a co-infection
Mycoplasma felis was most prevalent; Chlamydia felis was commonly co-detected with M. felis and produced severe systemic spread experimentally
Feline calicivirus was most prevalent; Chlamydia felis was not detected in any co-infected cats
Chlamydia felis was the most prevalent pathogen and always occurred as a sole infection causing conjunctivitis only
mcqs.e: Mycoplasma felis was most prevalent (24.75%), followed by FCV, Chlamydia felis (11.62%), FHV-1, and FeIAV. C. felis was co-detected with M. felis in 13/55 co-infected cats. Experimental challenge with an isolated C. felis strain caused severe conjunctivitis plus transient fever and systemic spread to multiple organs — confirming pathogenicity beyond conjunctivitis.

mcqs.q: Experimental Chlamydia felis infection in cats produced what unexpected finding regarding tissue distribution?
o: Infection was limited to conjunctival tissue with no systemic spread, confirming C. felis as a purely ocular pathogen
C. felis replicated in respiratory tissues and subsequently spread to liver, spleen, pancreas, kidneys, heart, and intestines
C. felis caused severe lower respiratory disease but spared the conjunctiva in experimentally infected animals
C. felis was rapidly cleared within 5 days of experimental inoculation, suggesting limited clinical significance
mcqs.e: High copy numbers of C. felis were found in turbinate, trachea, and lung tissues, with subsequent spread to the liver, spleen, pancreas, kidneys, heart, and intestines. This systemic distribution is broader than typically appreciated, reinforcing the clinical significance of C. felis beyond its classic association with conjunctivitis alone.

title: Feline leukemia virus in owned cats in Southeast Asia and Taiwan
authors: Capozza P, Lorusso E, Colella V, Thibault JC, Tan DY, Tronel JP, Halos L, Beugnet F, Elia G, Nguyen VL, Occhiogrosso L, Martella V, Otranto D, Decaro N
journal: Veterinary Microbiology
citation: Capozza P, Lorusso E, Colella V, Thibault JC, Tan DY, Tronel JP, Halos L, Beugnet F, Elia G, Nguyen VL, Occhiogrosso L, Martella V, Otranto D, Decaro N Feline leukemia virus in owned cats in Southeast Asia and Taiwan. Veterinary Microbiology. 2021. doi:10.1016/j.vetmic.2021.109008
abstract: Feline leukaemia virus (FeLV) is a retrovirus associated with fatal disease in cats with infection in its progressive form. The researchers assessed FeLV circulation across Southeast Asian countries and Taiwan during 2017–2018 using ELISA and nested PCR testing. Of 47 FeLV-positive cats, 32 were confirmed positive through molecular testing. Detection rates varied significantly by location, with frequency of occurrence of FeLV proviral DNA ranging from 0% (0/43 positive samples) in Indonesia to 18.5% (22/119 positive samples) in Thailand. Statistical analysis revealed associations between FeLV positivity and country origin, age, lifestyle, and oral mucosal abnormalities. The authors conclude that additional research is necessary to better understand FeLV distribution patterns across the region.

mcqs.q: A regional survey of FeLV in Southeast Asia and Taiwan revealed that prevalence varied substantially by country. What was the key finding about lifestyle factors?
o: Indoor-only cats had higher FeLV prevalence due to prolonged close contact with infected cage-mates
FeLV positivity was significantly associated with country of origin, age, lifestyle, and oral mucosal abnormalities
FeLV was not detected in any country outside Thailand, suggesting geographic isolation protects most populations
No associations between lifestyle factors and FeLV positivity were identified in this study
mcqs.e: Statistical analysis identified significant associations between FeLV positivity and country of origin, age, lifestyle, and oral mucosal abnormalities. FeLV proviral DNA frequency ranged from 0% (Indonesia) to 18.5% (Thailand), confirming substantial geographic variation with lifestyle as a contributing factor.

mcqs.q: What practical shelter and clinic implication follows from the regional FeLV variation found across Southeast Asia and Taiwan?
o: FeLV testing is not needed outside Thailand because prevalence is negligible elsewhere in the region
FeLV risk stratification should account for country of origin and lifestyle when evaluating cats from Southeast Asia
FeLV proviral PCR is unreliable in this region and ELISA alone should be used for screening
All cats from the region should be euthanized on FeLV diagnosis due to the progressive disease risk
mcqs.e: FeLV prevalence ranged from 0% to 18.5% across countries. When assessing cats from this region (e.g., international rescue transfers), country of origin, age, and lifestyle meaningfully affect pre-test probability. This supports FeLV testing in transit or recently arrived cats from high-prevalence areas as a standard-of-care consideration.

title: Seroprevalence and risk factors for Toxoplasma gondii exposure in Australian feral and stray cats using an in-house modified agglutination test
authors: Liyanage KLDTD, Amery-Gale J, Uboldi AD, Adriaanse K, Firestone SM, Tonkin CJ, Jabbar A, Hufschmid J
journal: Veterinary Parasitology
citation: Liyanage KLDTD, Amery-Gale J, Uboldi AD, Adriaanse K, Firestone SM, Tonkin CJ, Jabbar A, Hufschmid J Seroprevalence and risk factors for Toxoplasma gondii exposure in Australian feral and stray cats using an in-house modified agglutination test. Veterinary Parasitology. 2024. doi:10.1016/j.vetpar.2024.110306
abstract: Toxoplasma gondii is a globally distributed zoonotic protist, capable of infecting all warm-blooded animals. In Australia, cats (Felis catus) are the only definitive host capable of spreading T. gondii infection via oocysts. Free-roaming cats are widespread in Australia and can play a central role in the ecology of T. gondii. Therefore, understanding the epidemiology of this parasite in stray and feral cats is essential to understanding the potential risk of infection in animals and humans. Due to a lack of easily accessible commercial kits, an in-house modified agglutination test (MAT) was established to test for IgG antibodies against T. gondii, using cell culture-derived T. gondii tachyzoites, and compared with a commercial MAT. A total of 552 serum samples collected during 2018–2021 from stray (n = 456) and feral cats (n = 90) (samples with missing data n = 6) from four Australian states, representing different age groups of both sexes, were screened for antibodies against T. gondii. Risk factors for T. gondii infection were assessed using multivariable logistic regression analysis. The in-house MAT had excellent agreement with the commercial MAT and provided a reliable and economical serological tool for T. gondii screening in animals. The overall observed seroprevalence for T. gondii in cats was 40.4% (223/552). Bodyweight (as a proxy for age), geographical location, season and whether cats were feral or stray, were factors associated with T. gondii seropositivity in cats. Sex was not found to be a risk factor for T. gondii infection in feral and stray cats. This study shows that Australian stray and feral cats have a high T. gondii seroprevalence, which may translate to significant health impacts for wildlife species, livestock and the public.

mcqs.q: A serosurvey of 552 Australian feral and stray cats found approximately 40% seropositive for Toxoplasma gondii. What does this level of seroprevalence imply for public health and wildlife conservation?
o: Low risk, as most cats clear infection before shedding environmentally viable oocysts
Significant environmental oocyst contamination risk given that cats are the only definitive host in Australia capable of shedding oocysts
Moderate risk limited to urban areas where stray cats contact humans directly
Negligible risk because T. gondii in Australia affects only wildlife, not humans or livestock
mcqs.e: In Australia, cats are the only definitive host for T. gondii capable of shedding oocysts. A 40% seroprevalence across a large free-roaming population represents a substantial environmental contamination risk for wildlife, livestock, and humans — the core public health concern the paper raises.

mcqs.q: Among the risk factors examined for T. gondii seropositivity in Australian feral and stray cats, which was notably NOT significant?
o: Bodyweight (used as a proxy for age)
Geographical location
Sex (male vs. female)
Whether the cat was feral vs. stray
mcqs.e: Sex was not a significant risk factor. Significant predictors included bodyweight (proxy for age — older cats more likely exposed), geographical location, season, and feral vs. stray status. The absence of a sex effect means both sexes require equal consideration in public health risk assessment.

mcqs.q: An in-house modified agglutination test (MAT) was developed and compared to a commercial MAT in this study. What was the practical significance of this methodological development?
o: The in-house MAT was less sensitive, limiting its use to screening only
The in-house MAT provided a reliable and economical serological tool where commercial kits are inaccessible
The in-house MAT detected IgM antibodies, enabling acute infection identification unlike the commercial kit
The two tests showed only moderate agreement, so both should be run in parallel
mcqs.e: The in-house MAT showed excellent agreement with the commercial MAT and was developed specifically because commercial kits are not easily accessible in Australia. This makes large-scale, cost-effective screening feasible — important for epidemiological surveillance in resource-limited settings.

title: Renal alterations in cats (Felis catus) housed in shelters and affected by systemic AA-amyloidosis: Clinicopathological data, histopathology, and ultrastructural features
authors: Ferri F, Ferro S, Benali SL, Aresu L, Muscardin L, Porporato F, Rossi F, Guglielmetti C, Gallo E, Palizzotto C, Callegari C, Ricagno S, Mazza M, Coppola LM, Gerardi G, Lavatelli F, Caminito S, Mazzini G, Palladini G, Merlini G, Zini E
journal: Veterinary Pathology
citation: Ferri F, Ferro S, Benali SL, Aresu L, Muscardin L, Porporato F, Rossi F, Guglielmetti C, Gallo E, Palizzotto C, Callegari C, Ricagno S, Mazza M, Coppola LM, Gerardi G, Lavatelli F, Caminito S, Mazzini G, Palladini G, Merlini G, Zini E Renal alterations in cats (Felis catus) housed in shelters and affected by systemic AA-amyloidosis: Clinicopathological data, histopathology, and ultrastructural features. Veterinary Pathology. 2024. doi:10.1177/03009858241257903
abstract: AA-amyloidosis is frequent in shelter cats, and chronic kidney disease is the foremost cause of death. The aims were to describe kidney laboratory and microscopic findings in shelter cats with AA-amyloidosis. Cats were included if kidney specimens were collected post-mortem and laboratory data were available within 6 months before death. Renal lesions were evaluated with optical and electron microscopy. Mass spectrometry was used to characterize amyloid. Nine domestic short-hair cats were included; 4 females and 5 males with a median age of 8 years (range = 2–13). All cats had blood analyses and urinalyses available. Serum creatinine concentrations were increased in 6 cats and symmetric dimethylarginine was increased in all of the cats. All of the cats had proteinuria. Eight of 9 cats had amyloid in the medulla, and 9 had amyloid in the cortex (glomeruli). All cats had amyloid in the interstitium. Six cats had concurrent interstitial nephritis and 1 had membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. All cats had extrarenal amyloid deposits. Amyloid was AA in each case. Mass spectrometry confirmed amyloid was AA in each case. In conclusion, renal deposition of amyloid occurs in both cortex and medulla in shelter cats and is associated with azotemia and proteinuria. Renal involvement of systemic AA-amyloidosis should be considered in shelter cats with chronic kidney disease. The cat represents a natural model of renal AA-amyloidosis.

mcqs.q: In shelter cats with AA amyloidosis, which clinicopathological findings are universally present?
o: Elevated serum creatinine and normal urinalysis
Proteinuria and elevated SDMA in all cats; elevated creatinine in the majority
Hematuria and hypoalbuminemia in all affected cats
Elevated BUN with normal SDMA and absent proteinuria
mcqs.e: In this study of nine shelter cats with confirmed AA amyloidosis, all cats had proteinuria and all had elevated SDMA. Serum creatinine was elevated in 6 of 9 (approximately two-thirds). All cats also had extrarenal amyloid deposits. This pattern — universal proteinuria and SDMA elevation — supports using these as sensitive markers for renal AA amyloidosis in shelter cats, even before creatinine rises.

mcqs.q: What is the clinical relevance of identifying AA amyloidosis in shelter cats with chronic kidney disease?
o: AA amyloidosis is an incidental finding in cats with CKD and does not alter prognosis or management

AA amyloidosis should be considered in the differential for shelter cats with CKD, as it carries specific histopathologic lesions, is frequently associated with SDMA elevation before azotemia develops, and has a distinct pathophysiology from other CKD causes
AA amyloidosis is treatable with anti-inflammatory therapy, making early identification curative
The diagnosis requires mass spectrometry, making it irrelevant in routine shelter practice
mcqs.e: This study found that renal AA amyloidosis in shelter cats presents with both cortical and medullary amyloid deposits, universal proteinuria and SDMA elevation, and frequent concurrent interstitial nephritis. As AA amyloidosis is triggered by chronic inflammation common in shelter environments, it represents a distinct CKD pathway in this population. Recognizing it improves understanding of prognosis and supports targeted research into inflammation control to reduce disease burden.

title: Serial examination of the pancreas from shelter cats euthanized for population control for the prevalence of histologic and immunohistochemical changes
authors: Wu YA, Newman SJ, Lidbury JA, Steiner JM
journal: Veterinary Pathology
citation: Wu YA, Newman SJ, Lidbury JA, Steiner JM Serial examination of the pancreas from shelter cats euthanized for population control for the prevalence of histologic and immunohistochemical changes. Veterinary Pathology. 2026. doi:10.1177/03009858261451483
abstract: The clinical relevance of pancreatic histologic changes in cats is unclear. Determination of clinical relevance is complicated by the focal to multifocal nature of these lesions, variable clinical presentation of affected cats, and common comorbidities. Examining the histologic changes on serial pancreatic sections from a cohort of young adult shelter cats without externally observable clinical disease could inform what should be considered normal in cats. Pancreata were obtained from 48 cats euthanized for population control. While hypoalbuminemia was common, liver enzyme activity and gastrointestinal panel results were largely unremarkable. The pancreas was sectioned every 1 cm, routinely processed, and evaluated by a board-certified veterinary pathologist. Pancreatic histologic changes were uncommon in this cohort of cats. Hematoxylin and eosin-stained sections that showed lymphocytic infiltrates were recut for CD3 and CD20 immunohistochemistry. The distribution of CD3 and CD20 positive cells and their percentages were recorded. Of 48 cats, 13 cats (27%) had localized lymphocytic infiltrates with a median percentage of affected sections of 14% (range: 7%–92%). There were no differences in observed percentages or distribution of T- or B-cells. Scattered CD3+ T-cells were incidentally identified in intralobular parenchyma. As mild lymphocytic infiltration was uncommon in this group of cats, it may not indicate a physiological response, as the anticipated response to antigenic stimulation would be expected to occur more diffusely and more commonly. Thus, the role of these infiltrates may reflect bystander inflammation or a primary pathological process (pancreatitis) and likely varies depending on the specific disease context.

mcqs.q: A study of 48 clinically healthy shelter cats found that localized lymphocytic pancreatic infiltrates were present in 27% of cats with a median of only 14% of sections affected. What does this suggest about interpreting such lesions in feline patients?
o: Any lymphocytic pancreatic infiltrate in a cat should be treated as active pancreatitis requiring immediate dietary and medical management

Mild, focal lymphocytic pancreatic infiltrates can occur in clinically healthy cats, so their presence alone is not sufficient to diagnose clinically significant pancreatitis without additional clinical correlation
Absence of lymphocytic infiltrates on pancreatic histology rules out pancreatitis in all cases
Lymphocytic infiltrates in the feline pancreas are always a primary pathological process and indicate immune-mediated pancreatitis
mcqs.e: Lymphocytic infiltrates were found in 27% of clinically healthy cats, and were focal and limited in extent. The authors concluded these may represent bystander inflammation rather than primary pancreatitis. Clinical context—not histology alone—should drive diagnosis.

mcqs.q: This feline pancreas study used serial sectioning every 1 cm and found that distribution of T- and B-cells in infiltrates was not significantly different. What is the implication for understanding feline pancreatic inflammation?
o: Equal T- and B-cell distribution confirms a lymphoplasmacytic pancreatitis diagnosis in all affected cats

The lack of T- vs. B-cell predominance suggests the infiltrates are not clearly lymphoplasmacytic or T-cell-predominant, making their pathological classification uncertain and supporting a 'bystander' or incidental inflammation interpretation
Serial sectioning is unnecessary because single biopsy sections are sufficient to characterize pancreatic pathology in cats
Equal T- and B-cell distribution indicates a viral etiology and warrants infectious disease workup in every cat with pancreatic infiltrates
mcqs.e: No significant T- vs. B-cell ratio difference was found. This does not fit neatly into recognized immune-mediated pancreatitis classifications, lending support to the hypothesis that these are bystander infiltrates rather than a directed immune response, and cautions against over-interpreting incidental histologic findings.

title: Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza A(H5N1) Virus Infection in Cats, South Korea, 2023
authors: Kang YM, Heo GB, An SH, Lee H, Park E, Cha RM, Jang YY, Sagong M, Kim AY, Kim J, Lee EK, Kim SH, Lee K, Ku B, Lee YJ, Lee K, Lee KN
journal: Emerging Infectious Diseases
citation: Kang YM, Heo GB, An SH, Lee H, Park E, Cha RM, Jang YY, Sagong M, Kim AY, Kim J, Lee EK, Kim SH, Lee K, Ku B, Lee YJ, Lee K, Lee KN Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza A(H5N1) Virus Infection in Cats, South Korea, 2023. Emerging Infectious Diseases. 2024. doi:10.3201/eid3012.240154
abstract: In July 2023, cases of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) were reported at 2 shelters for stray cats in Seoul, South Korea. The cause of infection was suspected to be improperly sterilized raw food made from domestic duck meat, which was manufactured in South Korea. All viruses isolated from cats at the shelters and from the raw food belonged to HPAI A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b. The gene constellation of all viruses was most similar to that of viruses isolated in Korea in November 2022. Of note, the viruses isolated from infected cats harbored mutations E627K or D701N in polymerase basic 2, which are indicative of adaptation to mammals. Postmortem examination revealed systemic pathologic lesions and the presence of widespread virus in different tissues. Thus, consumption of raw duck meat contaminated with HPAI virus likely caused systemic symptoms and death in cats, indicating the introduction of mammal-adapted mutations of the virus.

mcqs.q: A 2023 South Korean shelter outbreak of HPAI H5N1 in cats was traced to what source, and what mutation pattern was found in isolated viruses?
o: Direct wild bird contact; mutations were absent, consistent with primary avian-origin infection
Improperly sterilized raw duck meat fed to shelter cats; viruses harbored E627K or D701N mutations in PB2, indicating mammalian adaptation
Contaminated water supply from a nearby poultry farm; viruses showed no mammalian adaptation markers
Cat-to-cat transmission from a single index case; viruses were phylogenetically distinct from any currently circulating poultry strains
mcqs.e: The outbreak was traced to improperly sterilized raw food made from domestic duck meat. Viruses from cats and the raw food belonged to HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b and harbored E627K or D701N mutations in PB2 — well-established markers of mammalian adaptation. Postmortem examination revealed systemic pathologic lesions with widespread virus in multiple tissues.

mcqs.q: The H5N1 shelter outbreak in South Korean cats illustrates a specific biosecurity risk for shelter medicine. What is the key takeaway?
o: All shelter cats should be vaccinated against avian influenza H5N1 as a routine measure
Raw poultry-based diets represent a concrete HPAI transmission risk in shelters and should be avoided or properly sterilized
HPAI poses no risk to cats that are housed indoors without direct bird contact
H5N1 in cats is always mild and self-limiting, so biosecurity escalation is unwarranted
mcqs.e: The outbreak was caused by improperly sterilized raw duck meat, not direct bird contact. Cats developed systemic, fatal disease with mammal-adapted viral variants. This is a direct evidence-based argument against raw poultry products in shelter cat feeding and underscores HPAI as a real biosecurity risk in facilities feeding raw meat diets.

title: Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza A(H5N1) Clade 2.3.4.4b Virus Infection in Domestic Dairy Cattle and Cats, United States, 2024
authors: Burrough ER, Magstadt DR, Petersen B, Timmermans SJ, Gauger PC, Zhang J, Siepker C, Mainenti M, Li G, Thompson AC, Gorden PJ, Plummer PJ, Main R
journal: Emerging Infectious Diseases
citation: Burrough ER, Magstadt DR, Petersen B, Timmermans SJ, Gauger PC, Zhang J, Siepker C, Mainenti M, Li G, Thompson AC, Gorden PJ, Plummer PJ, Main R Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza A(H5N1) Clade 2.3.4.4b Virus Infection in Domestic Dairy Cattle and Cats, United States, 2024. Emerging Infectious Diseases. 2024. doi:10.3201/eid3007.240508
abstract: We report highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) virus in dairy cattle and cats in Kansas and Texas, United States, which reflects the continued spread of clade 2.3.4.4b viruses that entered the country in late 2021. Infected cattle experienced nonspecific illness, reduced feed intake and rumination, and an abrupt drop in milk production, but fatal systemic influenza infection developed in domestic cats fed raw (unpasteurized) colostrum and milk from affected cows. Cow-to-cow transmission appears to have occurred because infections were observed in cattle on Michigan, Idaho, and Ohio farms where avian influenza virus-infected cows were transported. Although the US Food and Drug Administration has indicated the commercial milk supply remains safe, the detection of influenza virus in unpasteurized bovine milk is a concern because of potential cross-species transmission. Continued surveillance of highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses in domestic production animals is needed to prevent cross-species and mammal-to-mammal transmission.

mcqs.q: In the US 2024 HPAI H5N1 outbreak affecting dairy cattle and domestic cats, what caused fatal infection in the cats?
o: Direct contact with wild waterfowl migrating through the farm property
Consumption of raw, unpasteurized colostrum and milk from H5N1-infected cows
Cat-to-cat aerosol transmission from a single imported index case
Contact with H5N1-infected wild bird carcasses found near the farm
mcqs.e: Domestic cats fed raw (unpasteurized) colostrum and milk from H5N1-infected cows developed fatal systemic influenza infection. Infected cattle showed non-specific illness, reduced feed intake, and abrupt milk production drop. This established raw bovine milk as a novel cross-species H5N1 transmission route for cats.

mcqs.q: The detection of HPAI H5N1 in unpasteurized bovine milk in the US dairy outbreak has what implication for shelter and veterinary practice?
o: Commercial dairy products are now considered unsafe and should be avoided in all animal feeding
Cats and other companion animals should not be fed raw or unpasteurized animal products from farms near reported HPAI activity
HPAI H5N1 is unlikely to cause illness in well-nourished companion animals regardless of exposure route
Only cattle are at meaningful risk from H5N1 in commercial dairy operations; companion animals are not at risk
mcqs.e: The US FDA indicated the commercial (pasteurized) milk supply remained safe, but unpasteurized milk/colostrum was identified as a direct transmission route causing fatal feline H5N1 infection. This underscores avoiding raw unpasteurized animal-origin products in any companion animal diet, particularly in areas with active HPAI activity.

title: Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza A(H5N1) Clade 2.3.4.4b Virus in Domestic Cat, France, 2022
authors: Briand FX, Souchaud F, Pierre I, Beven V, Hirchaud E, Hérault F, Planel R, Rigaudeau A, Bernard-Stoecklin S, Van der Werf S, Lina B, Gerbier G, Eterradossi N, Schmitz A, Niqueux E, Grasland B
journal: Emerging Infectious Diseases
citation: Briand FX, Souchaud F, Pierre I, Beven V, Hirchaud E, Hérault F, Planel R, Rigaudeau A, Bernard-Stoecklin S, Van der Werf S, Lina B, Gerbier G, Eterradossi N, Schmitz A, Niqueux E, Grasland B Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza A(H5N1) Clade 2.3.4.4b Virus in Domestic Cat, France, 2022. Emerging Infectious Diseases. 2023. doi:10.3201/eid2908.230188
abstract: We detected highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b virus in a domestic cat that lived near a duck farm infected by a closely related virus in France during December 2022. Enhanced surveillance of symptomatic domestic carnivores in contact with infected birds is recommended to prevent further spread to mammals and humans.

mcqs.q: A 2022 French case report detected HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b in a domestic cat living near an infected duck farm. What surveillance recommendation followed?
o: All domestic cats in France should undergo annual H5N1 serological testing regardless of bird exposure
Enhanced surveillance of symptomatic domestic carnivores in contact with infected birds is recommended to prevent further mammalian and human spread
The infected cat was an isolated case and no changes to surveillance protocols were indicated
Domestic cats should be kept strictly indoors and vaccinated with available HPAI poultry vaccines
mcqs.e: The case demonstrates that proximity to infected poultry (even without direct feeding of raw bird products) can expose companion cats to HPAI H5N1. The authors recommend enhanced surveillance of symptomatic domestic carnivores near infected bird populations to detect and prevent further mammalian — and potentially human — spread.

mcqs.q: The France 2022 H5N1 domestic cat case, the South Korea 2023 shelter outbreak, and the US 2024 dairy cattle spillover collectively demonstrate what about HPAI H5N1 and companion animals?
o: H5N1 in companion animals is geographically limited to Asia and has not established transmission in Western countries
H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b poses a real and growing cross-species threat to domestic cats globally, via multiple transmission routes
Cats are resistant to severe HPAI disease because the virus primarily targets poultry
Companion animals can only be infected through raw poultry feeding, not through environmental exposure
mcqs.e: Across France (proximity to duck farm), South Korea (raw duck meat), and the US (raw bovine milk from infected cattle), HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b has caused fatal or severe illness in domestic cats via multiple exposure routes across multiple continents. This pattern establishes a genuine and growing cross-species public and veterinary health concern.

title: Risk Factors for SARS-CoV-2 Infection and Illness in Cats and Dogs
authors: Bienzle D, Rousseau J, Marom D, MacNicol J, Jacobson L, Sparling S, Prystajecky N, Fraser E, Weese JS
journal: Emerging Infectious Diseases
citation: Bienzle D, Rousseau J, Marom D, MacNicol J, Jacobson L, Sparling S, Prystajecky N, Fraser E, Weese JS Risk Factors for SARS-CoV-2 Infection and Illness in Cats and Dogs. Emerging Infectious Diseases. 2022. doi:10.3201/eid2806.220423
abstract: We tested swab specimens from pets in households in Ontario, Canada, with human COVID-19 cases by quantitative PCR for SARS-CoV-2 and surveyed pet owners for risk factors associated with infection and seropositivity. We tested serum samples for spike protein IgG and IgM in household pets and also in animals from shelters and low-cost neuter clinics. Among household pets, 2% (1/49) of swab specimens from dogs and 7.7% (5/65) from cats were PCR positive, but 41% of dog serum samples and 52% of cat serum samples were positive for SARS-CoV-2 IgG or IgM. The likelihood of SARS-CoV-2 seropositivity in pet samples was higher for cats but not dogs that slept on owners' beds and for dogs and cats that contracted a new illness. Seropositivity in neuter-clinic samples was 16% (35/221); in shelter samples, 9.3% (7/75). Our findings indicate a high likelihood for pets in households of humans with COVID-19 to seroconvert and become ill.

mcqs.q: In a household-based SARS-CoV-2 study, seropositivity rates were far higher than PCR-positive rates in both cats and dogs. What is the most important interpretation of this discordance?
o: PCR testing in pets is unreliable and should be replaced by serology for all SARS-CoV-2 surveillance
Many pets in COVID-19 positive households seroconverted (implying prior infection) without active PCR-detectable virus at time of testing, indicating past exposure rather than current shedding
Serology overestimates SARS-CoV-2 exposure in pets due to cross-reactivity with other coronaviruses
Pets primarily shed SARS-CoV-2 through feces rather than respiratory secretions, explaining low swab PCR rates
mcqs.e: PCR positivity was 2% in dogs and 7.7% in cats, while seropositivity was 41% in dogs and 52% in cats. This large gap indicates that most infections resolved before sampling — pets in COVID-19 households frequently seroconvert, meaning prior infection is common even when active shedding is not detectable.

mcqs.q: Which behavioral risk factor was associated with increased SARS-CoV-2 seropositivity specifically in cats (but not dogs) in the Ontario household study?
o: Cats that were allowed outdoor access
Cats that slept on their owner's bed
Cats fed raw diets in the household
Cats that shared a water bowl with other household pets
mcqs.e: Sleeping on the owner's bed was associated with higher SARS-CoV-2 seropositivity in cats but not dogs. Contracting a new illness was associated with seropositivity in both species. Close physical proximity to infected owners — especially sleeping contact — is a modifiable risk factor for human-to-cat transmission.

title: Genetically Similar High-Risk Strains of Carbapenemase-Producing Enterobacterales in Humans and Companion Animals, United States
authors: Xiaoli L, James AE, Stahl AL, Okumura M, Cole SD, Dietrich JM, Leeper MM, Putney JK, Walters MS, Stanton RA
journal: Emerging Infectious Diseases
citation: Xiaoli L, James AE, Stahl AL, Okumura M, Cole SD, Dietrich JM, Leeper MM, Putney JK, Walters MS, Stanton RA Genetically Similar High-Risk Strains of Carbapenemase-Producing Enterobacterales in Humans and Companion Animals, United States. Emerging Infectious Diseases. 2026. doi:10.3201/eid3203.251458
abstract: To elucidate the zoonotic potential of carbapenemase-producing carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CP-CRE) in US companion animals (i.e., dogs and cats), we queried the National Center for Biotechnology Pathogen Detection database to identify One Health clusters containing CP-CRE isolates from companion animals and humans. The 11 One Health clusters we found included most (69% [169/246]) publicly available CP-CRE sequences from US companion animals and were from 8 internationally disseminated, high-risk sequence types from 3 bacterial species (Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Enterobacter cloacae). All clustered isolates had New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase-family carbapenemases, and most (92%) carried the blaNDM-5 allele. The One Health clusters included several closely related subclusters with geographically linked isolates from both humans and companion animals. Those results suggest that CP-CRE is an emerging One Health issue and that direct or indirect transmission of CP-CRE is occurring between humans and companion animals in the United States.

mcqs.q: Genomic analysis identified 11 One Health clusters linking carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CP-CRE) from US companion animals and humans. What does this finding mean for shelter medicine practice?
o: CP-CRE in companion animals is exclusively acquired from human healthcare settings and poses no outgoing zoonotic risk
CP-CRE transmission is occurring between humans and companion animals, making shelter animals a potential source for staff, volunteers, and adopters
CP-CRE in companion animals remains genetically distinct from human strains, suggesting parallel but independent evolution
Only dogs carry CP-CRE; cats in shelters do not require AMR surveillance
mcqs.e: The One Health clusters show that genetically similar high-risk CP-CRE strains are shared between companion animals and humans in the US. Direct or indirect transmission is occurring — meaning shelter animals can be both recipients and sources of resistant organisms for humans in contact with them.

mcqs.q: All CP-CRE isolates in the One Health clusters from this study carried which carbapenemase type, and what is the relevance of this for treatment?
o: KPC (Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase) — treatable with newer beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations
OXA-48 — significant in Europe but rarely reported in North American companion animals
NDM (New Delhi metallo-beta-lactamase) — a metallo-enzyme not inhibited by clavulanate-type inhibitors, with very limited treatment options
VIM (Verona integron-mediated metallo-beta-lactamase) — most common AMR gene in shelter populations
mcqs.e: All clustered isolates carried NDM-family carbapenemases (92% specifically blaNDM-5). NDM enzymes are metallo-beta-lactamases not inhibited by standard beta-lactamase inhibitors, leaving very few treatment options — making prevention and infection control the primary strategy.

mcqs.q: What proportion of all publicly available US companion animal CP-CRE sequences were captured within the human-linked One Health clusters in this study?
o: A small minority (~10%), suggesting most companion animal CP-CRE is not shared with humans
About one-third (~30%), indicating occasional cross-species sharing
The majority (~69%), indicating that most companion animal CP-CRE in the US is genetically linked to human strains
Nearly all (~92%), identical to the proportion carrying blaNDM-5
mcqs.e: 69% (169/246) of publicly available US companion animal CP-CRE sequences fell within the 11 human-linked clusters. This is the majority — meaning One Health transmission is not a rare exception but the predominant epidemiological pattern for CP-CRE in US companion animals.

title: Giardia duodenalis in colony stray cats from Italy
authors: Guadano Procesi I, Carnio A, Berrilli F, Montalbano Di Filippo M, Scarito A, Amoruso C, Barni M, Ruffini M, Barlozzari G, Scarpulla M, De Liberato C
journal: Zoonoses and Public Health
citation: Guadano Procesi I, Carnio A, Berrilli F, Montalbano Di Filippo M, Scarito A, Amoruso C, Barni M, Ruffini M, Barlozzari G, Scarpulla M, De Liberato C Giardia duodenalis in colony stray cats from Italy. Zoonoses and Public Health. 2022. doi:10.1111/zph.12894
abstract: Study detected and genetically characterized G. duodenalis from stray cat colonies in central Italy (2018–2019). Of 133 fecal samples, 47 samples (35.3%) were positive for G. duodenalis cysts. Molecular analysis revealed 37 were positive for zoonotic Assemblage A and 2 showed a mixed infection (A + B). Sequence analysis identified Sub-assemblage AII and AIII variants. The authors noted all positive cats resulted to be infected with zoonotic assemblages, indicating stray cats as a potential human giardiasis source.

mcqs.q: A TNR program in Italy tests fecal samples from managed stray cat colonies and finds a substantial proportion positive for Giardia duodenalis. Molecular typing reveals all positive samples carry zoonotic assemblages. What is the primary public health implication?
o: The finding is of limited concern because Giardia in cats rarely causes human infection
Stray cat colonies may serve as a reservoir for human giardiasis, particularly for colony caregivers and others with contact exposure
Only cats with diarrhea should be considered infectious; asymptomatic carriers pose no zoonotic risk
The zoonotic assemblages found (A and B) are not transmissible via the fecal-oral route to humans
mcqs.e: The Italian study found 35.3% prevalence of G. duodenalis in stray cat colonies, with all positive samples belonging to zoonotic Assemblage A (sub-assemblages AII and AIII) or mixed A+B. Since all detections were of human-infectious assemblages, colony cats represent a potential source of human giardiasis—particularly relevant for caregivers, veterinary staff, and children with colony exposure.

mcqs.q: When managing a TNR program, Giardia testing and treatment protocols need to be considered. What does the Italian stray cat colony study suggest about the feasibility of relying on clinical signs alone to identify Giardia-positive animals for treatment?
o: Clinical signs are a reliable screening tool because most Giardia-positive cats show visible diarrhea
Clinical signs alone are insufficient—studies of asymptomatic colony cats can detect high prevalence, indicating subclinical carriage is common
Only kittens under 6 months show subclinical Giardia infection; adult cats with positive tests are always symptomatic
PCR testing of colony cats is impractical and fecal flotation is too insensitive to guide treatment
mcqs.e: The study detected 35.3% prevalence in colony stray cats through systematic sampling, not clinical presentation. This demonstrates that subclinical Giardia carriage is common—relying solely on clinical signs would miss a large proportion of infected cats and underestimate zoonotic exposure risk.

title: New insight into genetic diversity of zoonotic-potential Ancylostoma ceylanicum in stray cats living in Bangkok, Thailand, based on deep amplicon sequencing
authors: Jitsamai W, Kamkong P, Traub RJ, Taweethavonsawat P
journal: Zoonoses and Public Health
citation: Jitsamai W, Kamkong P, Traub RJ, Taweethavonsawat P New insight into genetic diversity of zoonotic-potential Ancylostoma ceylanicum in stray cats living in Bangkok, Thailand, based on deep amplicon sequencing. Zoonoses and Public Health. 2024. doi:10.1111/zph.13102
abstract: Study characterized hookworms from stray cats in Bangkok. Of 56 hookworm-positive fecal samples, 96.4% were identified as Ancylostoma ceylanicum and 1.8% as A. caninum. Deep amplicon sequencing of the partial COI gene revealed 19 haplotypes (AC01-AC19) with three considered zoonotic. The predominant haplotype AC01 was clustered with H01-a zoonotic haplotype. Researchers concluded that deep amplicon sequencing effectively determined genetic variation, zoonotic potential, and host-parasite relationships.

mcqs.q: A surveillance study of hookworms in Bangkok stray cats found 96.4% of hookworm-positive samples were Ancylostoma ceylanicum, and the predominant haplotype (AC01) clustered with a known zoonotic haplotype. What is the primary implication of this finding for public health surveillance?
o: The high prevalence of A. ceylanicum confirms that stray cats in Bangkok pose no zoonotic risk because this species is host-specific to cats
Stray cats in Bangkok are a significant reservoir of zoonotic-potential hookworms, with the predominant circulating haplotype genetically linked to a known zoonotic strain
Surveillance using standard fecal flotation is sufficient to characterize zoonotic risk from hookworms in stray cat populations
Genetic diversity among haplotypes indicates low hookworm transmission between cats and humans
mcqs.e: Of 56 hookworm-positive fecal samples from Bangkok stray cats, 96.4% were A. ceylanicum, with 19 haplotypes identified by deep amplicon sequencing. Three haplotypes were considered zoonotic, and the dominant haplotype AC01 clustered with H01, a known zoonotic haplotype. This demonstrates that Bangkok stray cats carry predominantly zoonotic-potential hookworm strains, making them a public health concern for communities with human-cat contact exposure.

mcqs.q: Deep amplicon sequencing of hookworms from Bangkok stray cats identified 19 haplotypes, with the predominant one clustering with a known zoonotic haplotype. What does this finding suggest for surveillance programs in urban free-roaming cat populations?
o: Standard morphological identification of hookworm eggs is sufficient for zoonotic risk assessment
Molecular characterization adds important information—species-level and even haplotype-level identification reveals zoonotic potential that cannot be assessed by conventional fecal examination alone
The high genetic diversity found indicates low transmission between cats and humans
Because A. ceylanicum is restricted to tropical Asia, these findings are irrelevant outside Southeast Asia
mcqs.e: The study demonstrated that deep amplicon sequencing of the COI gene could identify species, haplotypes, and zoonotic potential that are invisible to routine fecal flotation or even standard PCR. The predominant haplotype (AC01) clustered with H01, a known zoonotic haplotype, reinforcing the value of molecular surveillance for characterizing One Health risks in free-roaming cat populations.

title: Serological and Molecular Surveillance of Influenza A Virus in Dogs and Cats in Central Chile
authors: Baumberger C, Di Pillo F, Sanchez F, Sepúlveda A, Marambio V, Orozco K, Tapia D, Hamilton-West C, Sharp B, Schultz-Cherry S, Jiménez-Bluhm P
journal: Zoonoses and Public Health
citation: Baumberger C, Di Pillo F, Sanchez F, Sepúlveda A, Marambio V, Orozco K, Tapia D, Hamilton-West C, Sharp B, Schultz-Cherry S, Jiménez-Bluhm P Serological and Molecular Surveillance of Influenza A Virus in Dogs and Cats in Central Chile. Zoonoses and Public Health. 2026. doi:10.1111/zph.70073
abstract: Study evaluated influenza A virus circulation in companion animals from Chilean shelters and households (June–November 2020). IAV was detected by RT-qPCR in 3.2% (11/342) of dogs and 5.8% (4/69) of cats. Serological analysis revealed 55.5% (96/173) of dogs and 50.0% (10/20) of cats with IAV seropositivity. The study presented the first report of IAV detection in cats in South America and emphasized incorporating pets into surveillance frameworks under One Health approaches.

mcqs.q: A Chilean surveillance study found that molecular prevalence (RT-qPCR) of influenza A virus in companion animals was low, yet serological prevalence was high. What does this suggest?
o: The serological test was cross-reactive with endemic feline coronaviruses and the results are unreliable
Influenza A virus circulates in companion animals with higher cumulative past exposure than current active shedding rates suggest — many infections resolve before detection
Active influenza A infection in companion animals is clinically severe enough that all infected animals would present for veterinary care
Influenza A in companion animals is not transmissible and seroprevalence reflects maternal antibody transfer only
mcqs.e: RT-qPCR detected IAV in 3.2% of dogs and 5.8% of cats while seropositivity reached 55.5% in dogs and 50% in cats. This large discordance indicates widespread prior exposure with most infections having cleared by the time of sampling — similar to the pattern seen with SARS-CoV-2 in companion animals.

mcqs.q: This Chilean study presented the first report of influenza A detection in cats in South America. What broader surveillance principle does it reinforce?
o: Influenza A surveillance in companion animals is only necessary during active human influenza pandemics
Companion animals should be integrated into One Health influenza surveillance programs because they can harbor and potentially amplify circulating strains
Latin American companion animals have inherent resistance to influenza A strains circulating in Europe and North America
Shelter cats do not require influenza A monitoring because they have limited exposure to wild birds
mcqs.e: The detection of IAV in Chilean companion animals — and the first feline detection in South America — demonstrates that surveillance gaps exist in regions not traditionally included in influenza monitoring. This supports One Health approaches that incorporate shelter and companion animals as sentinels for circulating influenza strains.

title: Serological exposure to influenza A in cats from an area with wild birds positive for avian influenza
authors: Villanueva-Saz S, Martínez M, Rueda P, Pérez MD, Lacasta D, Marteles D, Ruíz H, Gonzalez A, Verde MT, Pardo J, Arias M, Peña-Fresneda N, Fernández A, Trotta M
journal: Zoonoses and Public Health
citation: Villanueva-Saz S, Martínez M, Rueda P, Pérez MD, Lacasta D, Marteles D, Ruíz H, Gonzalez A, Verde MT, Pardo J, Arias M, Peña-Fresneda N, Fernández A, Trotta M Serological exposure to influenza A in cats from an area with wild birds positive for avian influenza. Zoonoses and Public Health. 2024. doi:10.1111/zph.13085
abstract: A cross-sectional study of 183 stray cats in Spain from 2022–2023 measured anti-influenza A antibodies using ELISA. Four of the 183 animals tested showed anti-influenza A antibodies by ELISA, yielding a seroprevalence of influenza A of 2.19%. The researchers concluded that based on this low prevalence, cats did not have an important epidemiological role in influenza A transmission during this period.

mcqs.q: A Spanish study of 183 stray cats in an area with wild bird influenza A positivity found 2.19% influenza A seroprevalence. What conclusion did the authors draw about the cats' epidemiological role?
o: Cats in this region were important amplifying hosts for avian influenza A, warranting surveillance intervention
Based on the low seroprevalence, cats did not appear to play an important epidemiological role in influenza A transmission during this period
The 2.19% seroprevalence indicated widespread silent infection and the true burden was likely much higher
Stray cats in wild bird areas require prophylactic antiviral treatment to prevent influenza emergence
mcqs.e: With only 4/183 (2.19%) stray cats seropositive for influenza A despite being in an area with confirmed avian influenza positivity in wild birds, the authors concluded that cats did not have an important epidemiological role in IAV transmission during the study period. This provides useful baseline data for ongoing surveillance.

mcqs.q: How should the Spanish stray cat influenza A seroprevalence study be interpreted alongside the higher seroprevalence found in other species-specific or region-specific influenza surveillance studies?
o: Conflicting results across studies confirm that feline influenza A testing has no surveillance value
Low seroprevalence in stray cats near wild birds in this region suggests exposure risk is context-dependent and geographic variation in transmission is real
The 2.19% rate confirms that all stray cats worldwide carry influenza A antibodies at similar baseline levels
Low seroprevalence means stray cats should not be included in regional avian influenza control programs
mcqs.e: This study found low seroprevalence (2.19%) in stray cats despite proximity to influenza A-positive wild birds, while other surveillance studies have found higher rates in companion animals with closer human contact. This suggests that epidemiological risk is context-dependent — human-to-pet transmission routes may be more important than direct bird exposure in many settings.

title: Detection of SARS-CoV-2 and a possible variant in shelter cats
authors: Okwumabua O, Bradley-Siemens N, Cruz C, Chittick L, Thompson M
journal: PLoS ONE
citation: Okwumabua O, Bradley-Siemens N, Cruz C, Chittick L, Thompson M Detection of SARS-CoV-2 and a possible variant in shelter cats. PLoS ONE. 2025. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0317104
abstract: Researchers tested conjunctival, pharyngeal, and serum samples from 350 cats housed in an animal shelter, collected between July and December 2020, for SARS-CoV-2 using rRT-PCR targeting the N1 and N2 genes plus a surrogate virus neutralization test. Results showed that 203 (58%) swab samples were negative (N1 and N2 not detected), 2 (0.6%) were positive (N1 and N2 detected) and 145 (41%) were inconclusive (only N1 detected). Analysis revealed base-pair deletions and substitutions in the N2 probe binding region of the feline samples RNA extracts in comparison with the positive control. When using a redesigned cat-derived probe, 123 of 127 (96.9%) of the N2 negative samples returned positive results. The study concludes that cats can harbor the virus and serve as a potential source for virus spread, and suggests cats may carry a yet-to-be-described virus that is somewhat related to SARS-CoV-2.

mcqs.q: A shelter cat SARS-CoV-2 study found that using standard N2-targeting probes, many samples appeared inconclusive. When cat-derived probes were used, most of those reclassified as positive. What is the key diagnostic implication?
o: Standard human SARS-CoV-2 PCR probes are sufficiently accurate for feline surveillance and require no modification
Standard probes may under-detect SARS-CoV-2 in cats if the virus harbors mutations in probe binding regions, and feline-specific assay validation is important for accurate surveillance
The inconclusive results were due to poor sample quality, not probe design, and toothbrush sampling should replace swabs
The variant detected was not SARS-CoV-2 but a different feline coronavirus unrelated to the pandemic virus
mcqs.e: 127 samples with N2-negative results converted to positive (96.9%) when a redesigned cat-derived probe was used. Base-pair deletions and substitutions in the N2 probe binding region of feline samples suggest cats may harbor a SARS-CoV-2 variant with sequence differences that impair detection with standard human-designed probes.

mcqs.q: The finding of possible SARS-CoV-2 variants in shelter cats with altered N2 probe binding regions has what public health significance?
o: The finding is of no public health significance because SARS-CoV-2 cannot transmit from cats back to humans
Shelter cats may serve as a reservoir where SARS-CoV-2 variants emerge, with potential for spillback to humans — supporting continued feline surveillance
Shelter cats are protected from SARS-CoV-2 by their unique ACE2 receptor structure and do not require surveillance
The variants detected in cats are less pathogenic and pose no human health risk
mcqs.e: The study concludes that cats can harbor SARS-CoV-2 and may carry a related variant, and serve as a potential source for virus spread. Cats are susceptible, can transmit the virus, and shelter populations with high animal density and turnover represent a setting where viral variants could emerge and potentially spill back to humans.

title: A prospective study of mental wellbeing, quality of life, human-animal attachment, and grief among foster caregivers at animal shelters
authors: Powell L, Ackerman R, Reinhard CL, Serpell J, Watson B
journal: PLoS ONE
citation: Powell L, Ackerman R, Reinhard CL, Serpell J, Watson B A prospective study of mental wellbeing, quality of life, human-animal attachment, and grief among foster caregivers at animal shelters. PLoS ONE. 2024. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0301661
abstract: This longitudinal study examined 131 foster caregivers from five U.S. animal shelters between March 2022 and 2023. Participants completed three online surveys at baseline, during fostering, and post-placement. Key findings: positive affect decreased significantly after foster animals departed (p<0.01), particularly among dog caregivers. Negative affect remained stable throughout. Dog caregivers reported greater emotional and social/physical quality-of-life benefits than cat caregivers. Foster caregivers demonstrated secure attachment patterns with low anxious and avoidant attachment scores. Most caregivers (86%) indicated likelihood of future fostering participation. Caregivers reported experiencing both anticipatory and ambiguous grief upon animal departure. The researchers concluded that while fostering at animal shelters may serve as a One Health intervention by offering companionship, affection, and emotional support, mental wellbeing improvements were not evident, warranting caution about positioning foster care as a mental health promotion strategy.

mcqs.q: A prospective study of shelter foster caregivers found that after the foster animal departed, caregivers experienced:
o: Significant increases in both positive and negative affect
No meaningful change in positive or negative affect
A significant decrease in positive affect, while negative affect remained stable
A significant increase in negative affect and depression symptoms
mcqs.e: Positive affect decreased significantly (p<0.01) after the foster animal's departure, especially among dog foster caregivers. Negative affect did NOT significantly change. The effect was grief-like but one-sided.

mcqs.q: Despite reporting a significant emotional dip after fostering ended, the vast majority of foster caregivers said they would foster again. The key conclusion for shelter programs is:
o: Foster caregivers are resilient and do not require any emotional support from shelters
Shelters should promote fostering as a mental health intervention for isolated community members
Fostering is not well supported as a mental health promotion strategy, even though caregivers are willing to repeat it; emotional support around animal departure should be part of foster programming
The emotional dip is so minor that it does not warrant any programmatic response
mcqs.e: The study explicitly concluded that fostering should NOT be promoted as a mental health promotion strategy. The significant positive affect decrease — even though caregivers remain willing — suggests shelters should provide transition support at animal departure rather than marketing fostering as wellness-promoting.

title: Quantification of a shelter cat population: Trends in intake, length of stay and outcome data of cats in seven Dutch shelters between 2006 and 2021
authors: van der Leij WJR, Vernooij JCM, Vinke CM, Corbee RJ, Hesselink JW
journal: PLoS ONE
citation: van der Leij WJR, Vernooij JCM, Vinke CM, Corbee RJ, Hesselink JW Quantification of a shelter cat population: Trends in intake, length of stay and outcome data of cats in seven Dutch shelters between 2006 and 2021. PLoS ONE. 2023. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0285938
abstract: Shelters utilize metrics for self-assessment to enhance animal population health and identify disease outbreak risk factors. However, broader metric applications are needed for benchmarking and developing best practices. This retrospective study analyzed data from seven Dutch shelters over 2006–2021, examining intake sources, outcomes, and length of stay for over 74,000 cats. Key findings demonstrate that feline intake decreased by 39% per 1,000 residents, while euthanasia cases declined approximately 50%. Length of stay showed reducing trends, and return-to-owner rates increased alongside the risk-based live release rate. The researchers conclude these metrics effectively monitor shelter management, animal health and welfare, and can measure progress both nationally and across Europe.

mcqs.q: What trends in shelter cat metrics were observed across seven Dutch shelters over 15 years (2006–2021)?
o: Intake per resident increased while euthanasia rates remained unchanged
Feline intake decreased by approximately 39% per 1,000 residents and euthanasia declined approximately 50%, while live release rate and return-to-owner rates improved
Euthanasia rates increased due to rising disease burden among longer-staying cats
Intake and euthanasia were unchanged, but length of stay increased substantially
mcqs.e: Over 74,000 cat records showed feline intake fell ~39% per 1,000 residents and euthanasia cases declined ~50% across the study period. Length of stay trended downward, and return-to-owner and live release rates increased. These metrics collectively reflect improving shelter management and animal welfare across the Dutch shelter system. The study demonstrates that population-level metrics are valuable tools for benchmarking and identifying progress nationally and across Europe.

mcqs.q: Why are population-level metrics like intake rate, euthanasia rate, and length of stay considered valuable tools for shelter management?
o: They replace the need for individual animal health monitoring by providing a surrogate measure of welfare
